stories.headline: Essex gets £1.1m to tackle stalking
stories.summary: Stalkers across Essex will be offered help to change their behaviour. Victims get more specialist support, including help with online tracking.
body: Roger Hirst, the Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner for Essex, has secured £1,135,634 from a national Home Office fund for work with domestic abuse and stalking perpetrators. The money runs from October 2026 to March 2029. Your Harlow first reported the award.

The biggest share, £658,538, pays for a Stalking Intervention Service run by The Change Project, a charity that already runs behaviour change programmes for domestic abusers in Essex. It will work with people whose obsessive behaviour includes stalking, whether of a former partner or of someone they were never in a relationship with. The aim is to change that behaviour before it does more harm.

A further £338,015 goes to victims through Ending Violence in Essex, a partnership of local domestic abuse services that includes Changing Pathways and Next Chapter. Of that, £118,709 pays for a specialist in digital safety. They will help people whose stalker uses phones, apps or other technology to monitor, track or harass them.
"No one should have to change their route to work, stop seeing friends or feel unsafe in their own home," Mr Hirst said. "The test is whether people are safer after they come forward."

The money was announced in the same week the government said it would create a single criminal offence of stalking for England and Wales. It would replace the two stalking offences in force since 2012, after a review by Richard Wright KC found the law confusing. The maximum sentence stays at 10 years, and the change will be made when parliamentary time allows.
Mr Hirst called the single offence a positive step. But he said it had to be matched by a longer-term commitment to tackle what drives obsessive offending.

Essex Police dealt with 2,883 stalking crimes in 2024, according to figures it released under the Freedom of Information Act. That compares with 489 in 2018. Much of the rise followed changes to how police record stalking, including a 2020 rule that harassment between ex-partners is recorded as stalking unless officers are satisfied it is not.
Essex has had Home Office money for this work before. In 2023 the government named a stalking intervention project in the county among those backed by up to £1.7m from an earlier round of the fund.
The latest award was announced during the 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence, which runs until 10 December.

Anyone worried they are being stalked can call the National Stalking Helpline, run by the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, free on 0808 802 0300. Stalking can be reported to Essex Police on 101 or online. In an emergency, always call 999.

stories.headline: Stansted Airport Poppy Appeal raises record £26,190

body: London Stansted said on Friday 27 November that passengers, airport staff and visitors gave £26,190 to the Royal British Legion in the run-up to Remembrance Sunday. It is the most the airport's annual appeal has ever raised.
Last year's total was itself a record, and this year's beat it by more than £2,000. The money came in through a team of volunteers who stood with collecting tins and poppies across the terminal.
Volunteers covered 148 shifts of three hours each. Soldiers from the 33 and 35 Royal Engineer Regiments added another 64 shifts.

Simon Bambridge, the Royal British Legion's Poppy Appeal organiser, thanked the volunteers, staff and passengers. He said the appeal works only because so many people give their time, and that every donation helps veterans and their families.
## Next year's appeal

The Legion wants more volunteers for the 2027 appeal at the airport. Dan Turpin, the airport's community engagement manager, said the appeal is an important part of life at Stansted and that colleagues and passengers back it every year.

stories.headline: Essex's Prodigy star Keith Flint honoured with fossil snail name
stories.summary: Scientists have named a 99-million-year-old snail after the late Prodigy singer. Its hairy shell reminded them of his famous spiky hair.
body: A snail preserved in amber for about 99 million years has been named after Keith Flint, the Prodigy frontman who died at his Essex home in 2019. The new species, Archaeospirostoma flinti, was described in the journal Ecologica Montenegrina on 19 November.

According to the research team's release on EurekAlert, the hairs covering the shell reminded the authors of Flint's distinctive hairstyle. The hairs are part of the shell's outer protein layer. In this species they grow in flat fringes of equal length, unlike the single spikes seen on other hairy snails trapped in Burmese amber.

Dr Barna Páll-Gergely, of the HUN-REN Centre for Agricultural Research and Széchenyi István University in Hungary, led the study. He worked with Márton Szabó of Eötvös Loránd University and the Hungarian Natural History Museum, alongside the University of Szeged and the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
## What makes it unusual

The best-preserved specimen still has its operculum, the trapdoor-like cover a snail uses to seal its shell. Dr Páll-Gergely said its cone shape is "entirely unique" among this family's snails found in Burmese amber. The team says the snail lived on land, and the purpose of the cone-shaped cover is not yet clear.
It is the ninth member of its snail family found in Burmese amber, Mr Szabó said, and seven of the nine have hairy shells.

stories.headline: Frosty start gives way to a raw, grey Friday across Essex
stories.summary: A cold dawn leads into one of the chilliest days of the week across Essex. Rain and milder air arrive on Saturday.
body: The Met Office forecast temperatures around freezing across Essex overnight into Friday 27 November, with frost forming by dawn and a feels-like temperature as low as -4C for early commuters. No Met Office weather warning is in force for the county.
## A raw Friday

Friday looks the coldest day of the week. Harlow and Southend are forecast to reach only 3C under grey skies, with Colchester at 4C and Chelmsford at 5C. Rain edges into the west during the afternoon, with a 30% chance in Harlow around 4pm, while the east should stay dry. The wintry showers that appeared in some forecasts earlier this week have since dropped out.
The Met Office's East of England forecast says frost could form again in the east on Friday night, although the town forecasts put the lows at 2C to 3C.
## The weekend

Saturday turns milder but wetter, with cloud and rain for much of the day. Highs reach 8C in Colchester and 9C in Chelmsford, Harlow and Southend, with a 40% chance of rain. It will be breezy on the coast, with gusts of 30mph at Southend and 32mph at Colchester.
Sunday starts with mist and fog, then brightens with sunny spells and highs of 9C to 10C. Monday is milder again at 11C to 12C, though the Met Office says the wind will pick up.

Essex Highways has 55 gritting lorries ready for icy roads this winter, [as The Seax reported on Monday](/story/essex-gritters-55-winter-service-2026-27/). Forecasts can change, so check the Met Office page for your town before setting out early.

stories.headline: Harlow Council tells government to drop asylum plan for private homes
stories.summary: The Home Office's contractor wants to rent homes across Harlow for asylum seekers. The council's leader wants the plan dropped.
body: Harlow Council has demanded that the government abandon plans to rent private homes across the town to house asylum seekers. Your Harlow reported on Thursday 26 November that the council had received six letters in a single week from the Home Office's accommodation contractor. Each one proposes placing several asylum seekers in a privately rented home over the coming weeks.

Council leader Dan Swords said the council has objected to every proposal and expects many more to follow. He has written directly to the Home Secretary. He argued that hundreds of Harlow families are already living in temporary accommodation. He asked why the same homes could not go to local families who are homeless or struggling to find somewhere to rent.
## How we got here

Harlow has fought the Home Office over asylum housing before. In October 2025 the government told the council it intended to use Redstone House, the town centre block now called Endeavour House, for asylum seekers. Council papers show the building had earlier been shut as unsafe. Mr Swords wrote to the Home Secretary to oppose that plan and promised to fight it politically, legally and publicly. Your Harlow later reported that the proposal was withdrawn after the building's owners turned it down.

Renting ordinary houses is an approach the Home Office has tried elsewhere in Essex. Earlier this month villagers in Tillingham were divided over a plan to house six asylum seekers in a home there, [as The Seax reported](/story/tillingham-home-office-plan-six-asylum-seekers-house/).

Harlow's Labour group leader, councillor James Griggs, hit back on Thursday evening in a statement published by Your Harlow. He accused the Conservative-run council of trying to "outdo Reform" and of blaming asylum seekers for the town's housing shortage. He argued that the council's "Harlow Homes for Harlow People" approach covers only council-owned homes.
## What happens next

The decision on where asylum seekers live rests with the Home Office, not the council. Hannah Ellis, the Conservative parliamentary candidate for Harlow, has backed the council and called on the town's Labour MP, Chris Vince, to press the government. No Home Office response to the council's objections has been published.

Mr Vince replied on Thursday evening in a statement published by Your Harlow. He said the government had inherited a broken immigration system and pointed to the closure of asylum hotels and a fall in small boat crossings. He called Harlow a welcoming town and said people in genuine need should get protection, while those with no right to stay should be returned.
points: Six proposals arrived in a single week
The council says it has objected to every one
A 2025 plan for Endeavour House was withdrawn

stories.headline: Southend United legend Frankie Banks given Freedom of the City
stories.summary: The former Shrimpers full-back started the club's community work in 1991. The club says his impact goes far beyond the pitch.
body: Southend United great Frankie Banks has been awarded the Freedom of the City of Southend-on-Sea, one of the highest honours Southend City Council can give.

The club congratulated him on Thursday evening, sharing a picture of the Mayor presenting him with his framed Freedom scroll, made out to Francis Stanley Banks. It called him 'a Shrimpers legend who has had an impact far beyond the football pitch'.
Southend Today reported on 20 November that he and long-serving councillor David Garston were to be given the honour.
## From a park kickabout to Roots Hall
Banks was born in Hull in 1945, but his family moved to Hadleigh when he was a baby. A Southend United scout spotted him playing in a local park in 1958, when he was 13.

He signed his first professional contract at 17, in 1962, and made his debut away at Colchester United. In 1966 he joined his home-town club, Hull City, where he played more than 300 games in ten years. Hull fans later voted him the club's greatest right-back.

He came back to Southend in 1976 and played on until 1979. He then went straight into coaching at Roots Hall, working as youth team coach, first team coach, assistant manager and interim first team manager.
## 'Mr Southend'

In 1991 he became the club's first Football in the Community Officer, starting out on his own on £200 a week. That work laid the foundations of today's Southend United Community Foundation. He led it for 16 years before retiring in 2007.

Retirement has not slowed him down. In 1992 he set up the Senior Shrimpers club, which he still leads. It runs 12 day trips a year for more than 100 members aged 60 to 92, plus a Christmas party at Roots Hall.

He also runs walking football, mentors young coaches, helps with school PE lessons and tutors FA coaching courses for young people, the Foundation says. In 2014 he won the Football League Awards' Unsung Hero award.
When he turned 80 last year, Foundation chief executive Dale Spiby called him 'the heartbeat of this club and our Foundation'.
## A rare honour
Southend became a city in 2022. The late Sir David Amess, who campaigned for city status, was the first person to be given its Freedom, after his death.
The Music Man Project founder David Stanley was honoured in July 2023. Shrimpers manager Kevin Maher followed in 2024, becoming only the third person to receive it.
points: Signed professional for Southend in 1962
Voted Hull City's greatest right-back
Still leads the Senior Shrimpers club for over-60s

stories.summary: A teenager accused of murdering Radwan Shakur in Central Park has given evidence. He denies being part of any turf war.
body: The 17-year-old, who cannot be named for legal reasons, gave evidence at Chelmsford Crown Court on Thursday 26 November, BBC News reported. He and Blaise Mfinda, 18, deny murdering Radwan Shakur, 21, who died after being stabbed in Central Park, Chelmsford, on 12 June.

The boy told the jury he got the knife days earlier because he feared for his safety. He said he could not remember it touching anyone. The prosecution alleges a dispute over territory, which both defendants deny. The trial continues.

stories.headline: Colchester man admits 10 thefts from garage he was banned from
stories.summary: Danny Archer, 40, took £550 of meat and other food from the BP in Ipswich Road. He has been remanded in custody.
body: A Colchester man has admitted ten shop thefts from a city petrol station he was banned from entering, Essex Police said.

Danny Archer, 40, was arrested by officers in Colchester on suspicion of stealing from the BP service station in Ipswich Road between 1 and 18 November. He admitted ten counts of shop theft when he appeared before magistrates on Wednesday 25 November. The goods were meat and other food worth £550.

The court heard he was already under a five-year criminal behaviour order, imposed a year ago. It bans him from the garage and from four Colchester shops: the Co-op in Tamarisk Way, Greenstead, Tesco in Bromley Road, Tesco Express in St Christopher Road and Waitrose in St Andrew's Gardens.
Magistrates remanded him in custody. He will be sentenced at Ipswich Crown Court.

stories.headline: University of Essex students protest against MoD housing plan
stories.summary: Some students on the Colchester campus say they feel uneasy about living alongside soldiers. The university says nothing has been decided.
body: Students at the University of Essex's Colchester campus have protested against a plan to house 150 Ministry of Defence personnel there, the Daily Gazette reported on 26 November. Talks are still at an early stage.

Some students told the BBC they feared for their safety, as soldiers would not wear uniform on campus. Prof Chris Greer, the deputy vice-chancellor, said the university was still checking whether the idea is workable, [as The Seax reported when the talks emerged](/story/colchester-university-of-essex-army-personnel-student-accommodation/).

Prof Greer said a decision is likely within 12 months

stories.headline: Navestock fly-tippers targeted by Brentwood police van checks
stories.summary: Police and council officers are patrolling Brentwood's country lanes and stopping vans. The borough sees about three fly-tips a day.
body: Brentwood Neighbourhood Policing Team and Brentwood Borough Council's environmental officers have started a joint operation against fly-tipping, the council announced on Thursday 26 November. Officers are making extra patrols in the worst-hit parts of the borough and pulling over vans for spot checks.

Navestock and other quiet spots close to the M25 and A12 are being singled out by dumpers, the officers believe. Household rubbish, car parts and even burnt-out vehicles have been left at the roadside. Building waste has sometimes blocked roads altogether.

PC Tom Marriott is leading the police side of the operation. He said fly-tips had blocked entire country lanes, leaving rubbish that takes a long time to clear. Some people have dumped asbestos, which costs the council thousands of pounds to remove and can harm people and wildlife.
## What it costs

Clearing and disposing of dumped waste costs Brentwood Borough Council more than £95,000 a year, according to Councillor David Worsfold, who chairs its Clean and Green Committee. On top of prosecutions, the council hands out fixed penalty notices. A recent Brentwood case ended in a prison sentence, the councillor said.

In March the council reported that a man had admitted four fly-tipping offences across the borough, involving an estimated eight tonnes of waste. Neighbouring councils are also getting tougher. Epping Forest District Council crushed a seized fly-tipping truck for the first time this month, [as The Seax reported](/story/epping-forest-council-crushes-fly-tipping-truck-first-time/), and Basildon Council set up its own [fly-tipping task force](/story/basildon-fly-tipping-task-force-1696-dumps/) in November.
## How to report it

Anyone paying to get rid of waste should check the firm holds a waste carrier licence, PC Marriott said. Licences can be looked up on the Environment Agency website. A fly-tip happening now should be reported on 999. Dumped waste can be reported to the council with a photo and its exact location, for example from the What3Words app.
points: Clearing fly-tips costs the council over £95,000 a year
Fly-tipping fines can reach £50,000
Report a fly-tip in progress on 999

stories.headline: Leigh police stop finds £1m of cocaine as driver is jailed
stories.summary: Officers found 8kg in a car boot, then 7kg more in a Southend storage unit. Douglas Kramer got six years and eight months.
body: Douglas Kramer, 42, of no fixed address, Canvey Island, was jailed for six years and eight months at Basildon Crown Court on Thursday 19 November, Essex Police said. He had pleaded guilty to possessing cocaine with intent to supply.
Officers on patrol stopped his blue Vauxhall Astra in Bosworth Road, Leigh-on-Sea, at about 1pm on Monday 21 September. Police said the car was potentially linked to drugs.
In a cardboard box in the boot they found eight 1kg blocks of cocaine. Their enquiries then led them to a storage unit in Southend, where they found seven more.
All 15 blocks carried the same 'A-Y' marking and tested positive for cocaine. Police put the street value of the 15kg at more than £1 million.
In interview, Kramer told officers he was moving the drugs to pay off a drug debt. He refused to say who he owed. The court ordered the drugs to be destroyed.
## 'Taken out of circulation'
Detective Sergeant Leo Fordham, of the force's Serious Crime Directorate, called it 'an excellent stop' by Operational Support Group officers.

'Finding eight kilograms in the vehicle was significant, but our officers continued to follow the evidence,' he said. 'Drugs on this scale cause significant harm to our communities and generate money for those involved in serious criminality.'
points: Stopped in Bosworth Road on 21 September
All 15 blocks were marked 'A-Y'
Told police he was paying off a drug debt

stories.headline: Essex farmers raise fly-tipping costs at first county roundtable
stories.summary: Farmers told Essex County Council that rural crime and the cost of clearing dumped waste hurt them. More meetings are planned.
body: Fly-tipping on farmland and rural crime were the biggest worries raised at Essex County Council's first Farming and Rural Roundtable, held in November 2026. Farmers said clearing rubbish dumped on their land costs them money they cannot get back.

Essex County Council hosted the meeting. Farmers' groups attended, including Essex Young Farmers, the National Farmers' Union and the Countryside Land and Business Association. The Rural Community Council of Essex, the Farming and Wildlife Advisory Group, Natural England and Essex County Fire and Rescue Service also took part. Rising running costs, extreme weather and the security of water supplies were discussed too, the Bishop's Stortford Independent and Your Harlow reported.

Councillor Peter Harris, the Reform UK leader of Essex County Council, said agriculture "remains one of the foundations of our economy". Graham Harvey, who chairs the NFU in Essex, also welcomed the meeting.
The group agreed to meet every quarter for the next 18 months. Neither report gave dates for the next sessions or said what the council will do about fly-tipping on private land.
points: Hosted by Essex County Council in November
Roundtables every quarter for 18 months
Water security and extreme weather also discussed

stories.headline: c2c gets £2m plan to fix delays
stories.summary: Rail bosses are spending more to fix the Southend line after months of delays. Some December trains will finish early or be replaced by buses.
body: GBR Anglia, which now runs c2c alongside Greater Anglia and Network Rail's Anglia route, announced the extra £2m on Thursday 26 November. The money is meant to make trains between London and south Essex more reliable after a run of delays and cancellations this autumn.

Network Rail said the driest summer in 50 years dried out and shrank the clay under the tracks. That forced temporary speed limits on parts of the route. Signalling and power failures, a major fire at Stratford in August and a freight train derailment at Barking in October added to the trouble.

A Thameside Recovery Programme team has already laid more than 8,000 tonnes of ballast. In December a tamping machine, which packs the stones beneath the rails, will work through the night between Upminster and Benfleet. The aim is to lift the last speed limits before the new timetable starts on Sunday 13 December. Engineers are also strengthening the power supply so faults are found and fixed faster.
## What it means for passengers

Buses replace trains between Leigh-on-Sea and Shoeburyness on 5 and 6 December while lifts are fitted at Chalkwell and Southend East stations. From 7 to 11 December the last trains from London leave earlier than usual, such as 9.52pm via Laindon and 9.28pm via Tilbury. Some first trains into London run later from 8 to 11 December.

On 13 December the line between Upminster and Pitsea via Laindon is closed for engineering, with buses running between Pitsea and Shoeburyness. Trains on the Tilbury and Rainham lines still run direct to London. Network Rail said times may change and advised passengers to check c2c or National Rail before they travel.

Martin Beable, chief operating officer at GBR Anglia, said: "We know saying 'sorry' isn't enough." The company is also adding station staff, cleaning trains four times as often and planning more station work next year. [The Seax looked at how c2c fell from the top of the league tables](/story/c2c-best-in-britain-to-not-good-enough-investigation/) a day earlier.
points: Tamping machine works nights between Upminster and Benfleet
Buses replace Leigh-on-Sea to Shoeburyness trains on 5 and 6 December

stories.headline: Thurrock Council says no decision yet on selling 70 acres of open space
stories.summary: Three sites in Linford, Tilbury and Corringham could be sold. Residents have until 27 November to object, and cabinet would have the final say.
body: Thurrock Council has advertised that it intends to sell three areas of public open space covering almost 70 acres between them. The largest is about 60 acres west of Buckingham Hill Road in Linford, roughly the size of 35 football pitches. The others are 9.3 acres north of Parker Avenue in Tilbury and a third of an acre between The Manorway and Silvertown Avenue in Corringham.

Your Thurrock reported on Thursday 26 November that the council has stressed no decision has been made. A spokesperson said cabinet must approve any sale, and that the council is "not yet at that stage" for these sites. No sale price has been revealed, and the notices do not say what the land would be used for.
## Why the council has to advertise

Under the Local Government Act 1972, a council that wants to sell open space must publish its plan and consider any objections before deciding. Residents have been invited to object by 5pm on Friday 27 November. BBC Essex also reported the plan, describing a proposal to dispose of about 70 acres across three sites.
## Earlier sites

The Seax has found the council has used the same process for other sites. In October 2025 it advertised a lease of about 2,000 square metres beside the Flagship Centre in Tilbury, under a third of a football pitch, for a Youth Zone. In June, horse riders and walkers held a protest ride over a proposed sale of land at South Hill, near the Basildon border, and the Essex Bridleways Association objected.

Thurrock is still overseen by government commissioners. [Ministers said on Wednesday 25 November](/story/thurrock-council-minister-seventh-commissioners-report-assurance-plan/) that the council is much stronger but must still set a balanced budget for 2027/28 and keep paying down its debt.
points: Linford site alone covers about 60 acres
No sale price or future use has been given
Parker Avenue land in Tilbury covers 9.3 acres

stories.headline: Essex GP surgeries to offer 32,000 extra appointments this winter
stories.summary: NHS Essex is paying for 8,000 more GP appointments a month until February. It is part of a county-wide plan for the busiest season.
body: NHS Essex, the county's integrated care board, has put £1.1m into the extra appointments, which run from November 2026 to February 2027. Groups of GP practices across Essex will offer them, including in Southend and Thurrock. Depending on what a patient needs, the appointment may be with a GP, a nurse, a physiotherapist or another member of the practice team.

Michelle Stapleton, winter lead director at NHS Essex, set out the plan in an article published on Thursday 26 November. She said the money should help more people get care close to home. She also warned that it does not mean every pressure on local services will disappear.
## One plan for the county

Ms Stapleton said hospitals, GP surgeries, ambulance crews, mental health teams, councils, social care and charities are working to a shared winter plan. Health bosses keep a daily view of demand and spare capacity so they can spot problems early. Services can call on each other for help seven days a week when pressure rises.

She asked families who can help a relative leave hospital to talk to the ward team about practical support. That could mean arranging a lift home and making sure keys, food and heating are ready. Getting patients home safely frees beds for others who need them.
## The national picture

The government announced a separate £40m programme on 9 November to help GP teams reach patients most at risk of becoming seriously unwell. According to the Department of Health and Social Care, it is aimed at people with heart disease, frailty and lung conditions such as COPD, up to 300,000 patients across England. Ms Stapleton said NHS Essex is still waiting for details of what it will mean locally.
points: NHS Essex has invested £1.1m
Practices in Southend and Thurrock take part
Separate national £40m scheme targets high-risk patients

stories.headline: Rayleigh shoplifter jailed for five months after BP garage thefts
stories.summary: Stefan Jaworski, 44, stole £260 of meat, fish, chocolate and alcohol. A court order bans him from every BP in England and Wales.
body: A Rayleigh man has been jailed for five months for stealing from a petrol station he was banned from, Essex Police said.

Stefan Jaworski, 44, of Francis Walk, appeared at Basildon Crown Court on Wednesday 25 November. He admitted two thefts from the BP service station in London Road, Rayleigh, on 19 September. The goods were worth £260 in total.
He also admitted two counts of breaching his criminal behaviour order, which bans him from entering any BP service station in England and Wales. He was arrested by officers in Southend.
The order runs until 3 February 2031. It also bars him from every M&S store in England and Wales, the Sainsbury's Local in West Street, Rochford, and the Co-op in Spa Road, Hockley.

stories.headline: Tendring Local Plan with 18,173 homes heads to government inspector
stories.summary: Tendring District Council will send its blueprint for growth to the government by the end of December. Public hearings are expected in 2027.
body: Tendring District Council's full council voted on Tuesday 24 November to submit its new Local Plan to the government, the council announced on Thursday 26 November. The plan sets out where new homes, jobs and infrastructure should go across the district from 2026 to 2043.

A Local Plan is the document a council uses to decide planning applications. Tendring's has to meet the government's mandatory housebuilding target of 1,069 homes a year. The council aims to send the plan and its supporting evidence to the Secretary of State before the end of December. A planning inspector appointed by the government will then test whether it is legally sound.

About 320 people and organisations sent in around 1,400 comments during the final six-week consultation in September and October. Their worries included roads and traffic, pressure on health services and schools, drainage and wastewater, and the loss of countryside and farmland. Every comment from that consultation will go to the inspector.

Councillor Carlo Guglielmi, who chairs the council's Planning Policy and Local Plan Committee, said: "We know how deeply people care about the future of their communities." Council leader Mark Stephenson said the plan was key to lining up infrastructure with new building and to protecting communities from speculative development.
## What happens next

Public hearings are expected in 2027, and the inspector can recommend changes before the council adopts the plan. Some sites are already contested: Brightlingsea's ward councillors have vowed to fight Trinity College's bid to have land on the edge of their town included, [as The Seax reported](/story/brightlingsea-councillors-oppose-550-homes-church-road-local-plan/).
points: The government's target for Tendring is 1,069 homes a year
About 1,400 comments came in at the final consultation
The inspector can recommend changes before adoption

stories.headline: Stansted plane crash drill went well, airport and police say
stories.summary: More than 400 people rehearsed a plane crash at Stansted Airport on Tuesday 24 November. The services will now share what they learned.
body: London Stansted said on Thursday 26 November that its large emergency exercise had gone well, two days after more than 400 people rehearsed the response to a simulated aircraft accident. Operations director Nick Millar said the airport was pleased with how the day went. Chief Inspector Julia Finch, Essex Police's Stansted Airport commander, called it a very successful exercise.

Station Manager Amir Williamson, of Essex County Fire and Rescue Service's emergency planning team, said the drill tested the response at operational, tactical and strategic levels. Essex & Herts Air Ambulance clinicians worked through a scenario designed by their own team, with manikins and actors playing casualties. The organisations involved will now review the day and share the lessons.

Anyone near London Stansted on Tuesday 24 November may have seen a large number of emergency vehicles. The airport was running a full-scale training exercise that simulated a major aircraft accident, to check how its teams and the emergency services would cope with the real thing.

The drill took place at Compass Base, a remote aircraft parking stand away from the terminal, using a decommissioned aircraft. The airport said it had been planned so there is no impact on flights or passengers. Civil Aviation Authority rules require every UK certificated aerodrome to stage an exercise like this at least once every four years.

About 400 people took part. Airport teams worked alongside Essex Police, Essex County Fire and Rescue Service, the East of England Ambulance Service and Essex & Herts Air Ambulance. The British Red Cross, Uttlesford District Council and Essex County Council also supported it. So did the Rapid Relief Team, the Air Accidents Investigation Branch and the housing ministry, along with Ryanair, Border Force and National Express.

The scenario called for a long and complicated response involving many organisations. It was designed to test life-saving procedures, who takes command and how, communications, and the support offered to passengers, their families and others caught up in it.

Nick Millar, operations director at London Stansted, said an aircraft accident was "an extremely unlikely event". He added that it "remains the most significant emergency scenario we could face", so the plans must be tested regularly. He said the exercise would let the airport rehearse how it works with partners in a highly challenging situation and find ways to strengthen its response.

Chief Inspector Julia Finch, Essex Police's Stansted Airport commander, said: "We regularly test our plans and capabilities, and this is no exception." She said exercises like this make sure the force is ready for any eventuality, however unlikely, and that it has a really positive working relationship with the airport.
points: A decommissioned aircraft was used on a remote stand
The Civil Aviation Authority requires a full-scale drill every four years
Ryanair, Border Force and the British Red Cross were among those helping
stories.newAngle: the exercise is taking place today, Tuesday 24 November

stories.headline: Harlow G4S cash depot workers vote to strike before Christmas
stories.summary: Staff who move cash for banks and shops from Harlow have rejected a 1% pay offer. A walkout could hit cash machines.
body: Workers at the G4S cash depot in Harlow have voted to take strike action in the run-up to Christmas, the GMB union said on Thursday 26 November. The union said 95% of its members who voted backed industrial action. The staff transport and guard cash and valuables for banks and businesses.

The dispute is over pay. According to the GMB, G4S has offered a rise of 1% and has not improved on it. BBC News reported that the workers want 7%, in line with inflation, and that the union represents about 90% of staff at the site. The union points out that Christmas is one of the busiest times of year for shops taking cash.

The GMB warned that a strike could affect cash supplies to ATMs and businesses across parts of the South East and north and east London. No strike dates have been announced. Andre Marques, the GMB regional organiser, said the company needed to "get back round the table and make a decent offer".
## What happens next

G4S told the BBC it had not received formal notice of any strike. The company said it was open to talks with the GMB and hoped to reach an agreement without industrial action. Under rules brought in in February, unions must give 10 days' written notice of a strike, down from 14, and a ballot mandate now lasts 12 months rather than six.
points: 95% of GMB members who voted backed action
The workers are asking for 7%
No strike dates have been set yet

stories.headline: Essex this weekend: light trails, Christmas markets and switch-ons
stories.summary: Most towns have something festive on from Friday to Sunday. Many of the events are free.
body: Christmas takes over the Essex diary from Friday 27 November to Sunday 29 November. Light trails open, markets set up and several towns switch on their lights, with plenty of it free. Here is what is on, area by area, from The Seax's What's On listings.
## Chelmsford and mid Essex

Enlightened, the light trail at the Hylands Estate, opens on Friday, with entry from 4.30pm at the Writtle Gate. RHS Glow lights up RHS Garden Hyde Hall from 4.30pm to 9pm, and Lumina at South Woodham Ferrers runs from 4.30pm to 7pm, with tickets from £12.95. Cinderella opens at Chelmsford Theatre on Friday, with lines written by local children.

On Saturday, Christmas at Stow at Stow Maries Great War Aerodrome runs from 10am to 4pm, costing £5 for adults with under-16s free. That evening Chelmsford Cathedral marks 40 years of The Glory with a textile evening from 6.15pm, at £7.50.
## Southend and south Essex

Light Up Leigh fills Leigh Community Centre and the library gardens on Friday from 3pm to 8pm, with carols at 6pm and free entry. Adventure Island's Wonderland opens on Saturday from 10am, from £20, or £10 for annual pass holders. Canvey Island's Christmas event runs from noon to 5pm on Saturday. Barleylands near Billericay has its Christmas markets, and Scott's Light Up the Night in Rochford costs £7.
## Colchester, Braintree and the coast

Halstead switches on its lights in the Public Gardens at 4pm on Saturday, with Santa's grotto from 2pm and jazz from 4.30pm. Dedham's Christmas market fills Royal Square from 12.30pm to 4.30pm that day, with free entry. Clacton Pier opens Santa's Enchanted Grotto on Saturday, while Colchester Zoo's Enchanted Trail of Light runs in the evenings. Colchester United holds a Christmas fair at the JobServe Community Stadium on Sunday.
## West Essex and Uttlesford

Saffron Walden's late-night shopping evening is on Friday, [with free town council buses from 4pm to 8pm](/story/saffron-walden-free-christmas-shopper-buses-27-november-4-december/). On Sunday, Ingatestone's festive fair runs along the High Street from noon to 5pm. Ongar's Christmas festival starts at 2pm, with its lights switched on at 7pm, and both are free. In Harlow, the Merry Minds festive fun run for Mind in West Essex starts at The Water Gardens at 10am on Sunday.
points: Light Up Leigh on Friday is free, with carols at 6pm
Halstead's lights go on at 4pm on Saturday
Ongar switches on its lights at 7pm on Sunday

stories.headline: Essex patrols targeting predatory behaviour made 128 arrests in a year
stories.summary: The figures come as the force marks 16 Days of Activism. Its chief constable says tackling violence against women matters every day.
body: Essex Police officers on Operation Vigilant made 128 arrests over the last year, the force said, as it joined the global 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence.

Op Vigilant puts officers alongside CCTV operators and local partners to spot concerning and predatory behaviour in public places and step in early. In the last year 811 officers took part, with more than 2,500 interactions and 1,261 vehicles stopped, according to Chief Inspector Sam Girdlestone, the force's tactical lead on violence against women and girls.
Teams are being sent where they can have most impact across the county in the run-up to Christmas and through the festive period, the force said. The campaign runs until 10 December.
## 'This matters every day'
Chief Constable Rachel Nolan, who has served with Essex Police for more than 27 years, said every woman and girl should be able to go about her life without fear of violence, abuse or harassment.

'Awareness events give us an important opportunity to stop, reflect and talk about these issues,' she said. 'But I want to be clear that, for us, this is about far more than marking a moment in the calendar.'
## Rape cases and new protection orders

The force says Operation Soteria, brought in across Essex in February 2025, puts more scrutiny on suspects in rape and serious sexual offence investigations. It says rape solved rates have improved since, working with the Crown Prosecution Service.

Domestic Abuse Protection Orders are also being rolled out more widely. They let police and partners place restrictions and requirements on people suspected of domestic abuse. Each month an Essex Stalking Intervention Panel brings police and partner agencies together to look at individual stalking cases.
## Help to change

The force's Reflect campaign is aimed at people who recognise controlling, coercive, stalking or other abusive behaviour in themselves. It urges them to get help to change through Essex Compass, at essexcompass.org.uk or on 0330 333 7444.
points: 811 officers took part in Op Vigilant
1,261 vehicles stopped
Help to change: Essex Compass, 0330 333 7444

stories.headline: Southend Airport gets easyJet flights to Corfu from May
stories.summary: Holidaymakers in south Essex will be able to fly direct to the Greek island next summer. Tickets are already on sale.
body: London Southend Airport announced on Thursday 26 November that easyJet will fly to Corfu twice a week from 11 May 2027. Flights will run on Tuesdays and Saturdays through the summer, and easyJet holiday packages are on sale too.

It is easyJet's second route between Southend and Greece, after the Rhodes service announced in September. The airport said new routes to Belfast City, Budapest, Edinburgh, Lyon, Rhodes and Sharm El Sheikh all start within the next 12 months, giving it a network of 31 destinations. Swiss carrier [Chair Airlines' daily Zurich flights](/story/southend-airport-chair-airlines-zurich-daily-flights/) are also on sale for spring.

According to the airport, Southend was the UK's fastest-growing airport in 2025, with passenger numbers up 150% on 2024. It said its average delay that year was 10 minutes and 24 seconds, the second best in the country.

Nigel Mayes, the airport's business development director, called Corfu "a fantastic addition to our growing network". Kevin Doyle, easyJet's UK country manager, said the airline looked forward to welcoming customers on board from May.
points: Flights run on Tuesdays and Saturdays
Rhodes is easyJet's other Greek route from Southend
Belfast City, Budapest and Lyon routes also start within a year

stories.headline: Cocaine kingpin who sent couriers to Harwich and Southend jailed for 18 years
stories.summary: Bradley Stainer ran a network that moved more than a tonne of cocaine. His couriers were paid more than £1,000 a day.
body: A man who ran a nationwide cocaine network, whose couriers made regular trips to Harwich Port, has been jailed for 18 years.

Bradley Stainer, 46, of Gatton Park Road, Redhill, was sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Wednesday 25 November. He had admitted conspiracy to supply cocaine and possession of criminal property in June.
The Metropolitan Police says the network moved more than a tonne of cocaine into the UK. Stainer bought the drug on a commercial scale and used a team of couriers to move it around the country.
## The Essex link

Detectives tracked the couriers between April and November 2023. They found regular trips to Harwich Port, as well as journeys to Southend, South London, Rotherham, Leicester, Walsall and other places.

Packages of imported cocaine were collected and driven across London and the rest of the UK, as far as Bradford, Birmingham, Bristol and Cardiff. The Met has not said what the trips to Harwich involved.
## A grandmother's courier gang

The couriers were run by Deborah Mason, 66, of Crayford Road, Tufnell Park, who recruited members of her own family. She was convicted of conspiracy to supply Class A drugs in April 2025 and jailed for 20 years that July.

Mason and seven other members of the gang were jailed for a total of 106 and a half years at Woolwich Crown Court. The court heard they supplied nearly a tonne of cocaine over seven months, with a street value of about £80 million.

Stainer, who called himself "Bugsy", contacted the group through encrypted messaging apps, including Signal, and used false names. He agreed their pay, more than £1,000 a day, and told them where to go.

He travelled between the UK and Spain, leaving with large amounts of cash hidden in his luggage and taking the profits back to his home in Marbella. Messages showed he and Mason also talked about spending time in Dubai and Marbella.
## How he was caught

Officers went through thousands of encrypted messages, mapped the whole network and kept the gang under surveillance. The messages kept mentioning a man called "Bugsy", who arranged wages, directed shipments and collected money every month.
Detectives linked the alias to Stainer and showed that he was the head of the operation. He was arrested on 19 May.
Detective Constable Jack Kraushaar, who led the investigation, said officers had "scoured through thousands of encrypted messages and identified Stainer as the next link in the chain".
"This is more evidence of the Met's battle to prevent more drugs entering the UK, where they cause violence, antisocial behaviour and tear communities apart," he said.
points: Unmasked as "Bugsy" through encrypted messages
Ringleader Deborah Mason jailed for 20 years in 2025
Arrested on 19 May after the gang's convictions

stories.headline: Chelmsford Local Plan hearings finish, with final day cancelled
stories.summary: Public hearings on Chelmsford's plan for future homes and jobs have ended. Inspectors will now decide what changes it needs.
body: The public hearings into Chelmsford's new Local Plan have closed, Chelmsford City Council said on Thursday 26 November. Planning inspectors have cancelled the last session, which had been due the following Tuesday.

A Local Plan sets out where new homes, jobs, roads and schools should go in the years ahead. Before a council can use it to judge planning applications, independent inspectors must decide that it is legally compliant and sound.

Hearings were held at Chelmsford Civic Centre over several sessions in November, [as The Seax reported when they opened](/story/chelmsford-local-plan-examination-hearings-begin/). They covered housing, jobs, transport, infrastructure, the environment and the protection of valued landscapes and heritage. The inspectors decided the last two topics, design and monitoring policies, can be dealt with in writing instead. People who could not attend in person sent written comments, which count as evidence.
Councillor Richard Lee, the council's cabinet member for planning and place-shaping, said the plan "reflects our shared ambitions for Chelmsford" and thanked everyone who took part.
## What happens next

The inspectors will now weigh the evidence and say what main modifications, or changes, the plan needs to be sound. Chelmsford City Council will then publish those changes for public consultation. The inspectors will read the responses before writing their final report. The council has not given dates for any of these steps.
points: Design and monitoring policies will be settled in writing
Changes the inspectors want will go out to public consultation
No date yet for the inspectors' final report
stories.newAngle: The hearings closed on 26 November and the 1 December session was cancelled, with the last two topics moved to written evidence.

stories.headline: Southend's Cliffs Pavilion unveils new foyer, bars and restaurant
stories.summary: The Westcliff theatre's first big makeover since the 1990s is finished. Government levelling up money helped pay for it.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council unveiled the refurbished Cliffs Pavilion in Westcliff-on-Sea on Thursday 26 November. Its new foyer, bars and restaurant opened to audiences for the first time that day, according to Trafalgar Entertainment, which runs the theatre for the council.
## What has changed

Visitors now walk into a redesigned foyer with a café by day that turns into a bar on show nights. The box office is bigger, easier to use and back beside the main entrance. There is a new merchandise counter, a sweet kiosk open to all and a new suite of women's toilets on the ground floor.

Upstairs, the Pavilion restaurant has been extended and modernised, with more seats and its own bar. A new café bar in the lobby serves light lunches, coffee and cake during the day, with USB points for people who want to work there. Trafalgar said room for pre-show and interval drinks has almost doubled.
## Who paid

Work began in 2024 and shows carried on throughout. It is the first major work on the venue, which is more than 60 years old, since the 1990s. The project was backed by £5.5m from the government's Levelling Up Fund, with more money from the council, which owns the building, and from Trafalgar. Neither has said what the total bill came to.
Councillor Matt Dent, the council's cabinet member for business, culture, music and tourism, called the Cliffs Pavilion "one of Southend's most iconic landmarks".
## What happens next

Pre-show dining returns for the Christmas pantomime. Oliver Stacey, venue director at Southend Theatres, said a new pre-show menu launches with the restaurant, and a pantomime brunch is being added before selected afternoon performances.
points: Drinks space before shows and at the interval almost doubles
Box office moves back beside the main entrance
Pantomime brunch added before selected afternoon shows

stories.headline: Great Waltham concert to fund generators for Ukraine's winter
stories.summary: Ukrainian accordionist Igor Saienko plays the village church on 9 December. Entry is free, with donations going to a Felsted charity which helps fund generators for Ukraine.
body: A leading Ukrainian accordionist is coming to Great Waltham next month to raise money for portable generators, as families in Ukraine face another winter with little heat or power.

Igor Saienko, a soloist with the National Philharmonic of Ukraine, plays Great Waltham Church on Wednesday 9 December. Doors open at 7pm for a 7.30pm start, and the programme mixes popular classics with festive music.
Entry is free, but the audience is asked to give towards the generators. Gift Aid is available, and refreshments will be served in the interval.
Organisers say many Ukrainians face the winter with limited heat and electricity, often in ageing apartment blocks where temperatures fall well below freezing.
## The music

Saienko plays the bayan, the button accordion of Eastern Europe. He was a member of the Mykola Rizol Bayan Quartet of the National Philharmonic of Ukraine from 2002 to 2023, and its artistic director from 2016 to 2019.

He also co-founded the Kyiv Classic Accordion duo and made his UK debut in Glasgow in 2023, with a chamber ensemble from the Royal Scottish National Orchestra. He has held the honorary title of Merited Artist of Ukraine since 2010.
He is touring the UK to raise money for the appeal. His second Essex date is at St Mary's Church, Stebbing, on Thursday 10 December.
## The Felsted charity behind the generators

The generators will be supplied by UK-Aid, the working name of Felsted Aid for Deprived Children. Alan Hilliar and Pauline Craven started the charity in 2001, and it became a registered charity in 2003.

It has supported the Revival Centre in Chernihiv, northern Ukraine, since 2001. The centre was set up to help children affected by the Chernobyl disaster, and now helps disabled and sick children get specialist treatment. The charity also sends humanitarian aid to vulnerable families.
In its latest accounts with the Charity Commission, UK-Aid reported three aid trips that took 98,624 kilos of supplies to Ukraine.
People who cannot get to the concert can donate on the UK-Aid website, adding "Generators" in the "Write a Note" box. The concert is organised by the Great Waltham Community Network.
points: Doors 7pm for a 7.30pm start
Second concert at Stebbing on 10 December
Donations buy portable generators

stories.summary: The bakery chain has opened on Leigh-on-Sea's Broadway. Nearly 2,000 people had signed a petition against it.

stories.headline: Southend's Lazydays adds Ella Eyre, KT Tunstall and Pixie Lott for 2027
stories.summary: Sigala, Daniel Bedingfield and Celebrity Traitors winner Bash Croft are also on the biggest line-up announcement yet for the Priory Park festival, which returns in July 2027.
body: Southend's Lazydays Festival has named the next wave of acts for summer 2027, in what its organisers call their biggest line-up announcement yet. They join headliners Dizzee Rascal, Kaiser Chiefs and Olly Murs at Priory Park from Friday 23 to Sunday 25 July 2027. Madness open the week with a separate concert on the Thursday.
The festival expects more than 22,000 attendances across the four days. About 8,000 people went in 2025 and more than 12,000 in 2026, Your Southend has reported.
## Who is coming
BRIT Award winner Ella Eyre brings her full band and her UK number one Waiting All Night. Grammy-nominated Scottish singer KT Tunstall adds Suddenly I See and Black Horse and the Cherry Tree.
Pixie Lott joins her fellow Essex-raised pop star Olly Murs for what the festival calls a homecoming Sunday.

For dance fans, Sigala plays a set of anthems and Jaguar Skills takes over The Big Hop Stage. Lottery Winners arrive fresh from supporting Robbie Williams on his stadium tour, and Daniel Bedingfield brings Gotta Get Thru This.

Lazydays says it is the first UK festival to book Bash Croft for 2027. The Heartstopper actor won BBC One's The Celebrity Traitors and released his debut EP, The Great Forever, in November. The Amy Winehouse Band, made up of musicians who played with the late singer, is also on the bill. Issey Cross brings drum and bass to the festival for the first time.
## Room for local talent
Rising artists Girl in the Year Above, The Bracknall, Grace Gachot and Abby T are booked, alongside homegrown acts Cuckoo Corner and Nemesis. The Breakwater Stage will again showcase new talent.
## Madness on the opening night

The Madness concert on Thursday 22 July is ticketed separately. Peter Hook and The Light, The Selecter, The Undertones, Hak Baker, David Rodigan, Dub Pistols, Ed Rome, Gentleman's Dub Club and The Skints support. Grapevine reported in November that 90% of tickets had already gone.
## How it started

Three friends from Southend launched Lazydays in 2024: Andy Williamson, Elliott Waters and Mike Forster-Bromfield. David Rodigan headlined that first year. The 2026 headliners were Tinie Tempah, Feeder and Sister Sledge.

"This is where people really start to see the scale of what we're creating for 2027," said Elliott Waters, co-founder and artistic director. "Lazydays has never just been about the music. It's the atmosphere, the food and drink, the unexpected moments."
## What else is new

For the first time there will be an off-site campsite, with shuttle buses to Priory Park. The Thirsty Moose festival pub, silent disco, Bangers Bingo, vintage rides and VIP garden all return, with comedy, street theatre and local street food. Children under six get in free.
## Tickets

Weekend tickets start at £149.95, weekend camping tickets at £194.45 and day tickets at £54.95, all plus booking fees. Payment plans start at £35 a month for a weekend ticket and £10 a month for a day ticket. More acts and attractions are due to be announced in the coming months, at lazydaysfestival.com.
points: Headliners Dizzee Rascal, Kaiser Chiefs and Olly Murs
More than 22,000 attendances expected over four days
First off-site campsite, with shuttles to the park
Under-sixes go free

stories.headline: Greater Anglia to give unclaimed lost property to Essex women's refuges
stories.summary: Refuges across Essex can now ask Greater Anglia for items left on its trains. Deliveries go through lockers to keep refuge addresses secret.
body: Women's refuges in Essex, Suffolk, Cambridgeshire and Greater London can now send Greater Anglia a list of things they need. The train company will then supply what it can from unclaimed lost property. The trial, announced on Thursday 26 November, makes Greater Anglia the second train operator to join a scheme the Rail Delivery Group began with Southeastern in November 2025.

Rail UK reported that the first Greater Anglia delivery included toiletries and other personal items. Refuges can also ask for things such as clothing or toys. Parcels travel through InPost lockers, so nobody handling them learns where a refuge is.
According to RailAdvent, Greater Anglia keeps lost property for three months. Only after that can unclaimed belongings be donated or disposed of, and that policy has not changed.

Lynsey Flack, Greater Anglia's head of customer service, said things left on trains and stations "can often still be useful to someone else". She thanked the company's lost property team at Pakex, the Rail Delivery Group and InPost. Dan Mann, co-chief executive of the Rail Delivery Group, said the scheme builds on the success of the first trial.
## How the scheme began

Southeastern started it with the London charity Solace Women's Aid. The Rail Delivery Group said that first delivery, in November 2025, held coats, jumpers and cuddly toys. Solace supported 817 women and children across 19 refuges and 71 move-on spaces in its most recent year, the group said at the time.

Railway companies already run Rail to Refuge with Women's Aid. It gives people escaping domestic abuse a free train journey to a refuge, and the Rail Delivery Group says 13,054 survivors have used it since April 2020.
Neither company has said how long the Greater Anglia trial will run. The Rail Delivery Group has said it wants to bring more train operators into the scheme.
points: Refuges in Suffolk, Cambridgeshire and Greater London are covered too
Unclaimed items are held for three months first
Rail to Refuge has given 13,054 survivors free travel since April 2020

stories.headline: South Essex crisis team uses charity kit to keep older patients at home
stories.summary: A south Essex NHS crisis team has bought puzzles, music and craft kits with charity money. They help older patients stay out of hospital.
body: Older people in a mental health crisis in Southend, Basildon and Chelmsford now have extra practical help at home. Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT) said on Thursday 26 November that its own charity had paid for the kit.

EPUT's Functional Intensive Response and Support Team, known as FIRST, visits older adults in their own homes. It works with families and other clinical teams so patients can manage their mental health and, where possible, avoid going into hospital.

The charity money bought whiteboards and pens, notebooks, large-print puzzles, craft materials, portable CD players and CDs, and sensory items such as fidget toys and stress putty. Occupational therapists share them across the FIRST teams in Southend, Basildon and Chelmsford.

Laura Dawson, an occupational therapist with the team, said the resources had been "really beneficial for our patients". She said whiteboards can work as memory prompts or help someone plan a daily routine. Silk painting has worked especially well, she said, because people can quickly make something they feel proud of.

Families can also try an item before deciding to buy one themselves. EPUT Charitable Funds pays for activities and improvements beyond what the NHS would normally fund. Anyone in a mental health crisis can call EPUT's 24-hour crisis line on 111.
points: FIRST visits older adults in their own homes
Silk painting has proved one of the most effective activities
Paid for by EPUT Charitable Funds, not core NHS budgets
The 111 mental health crisis line runs 24 hours a day
stories.source: Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust

stories.headline: Castle Point MP takes Green Belt housing worries to the Commons
stories.summary: Dame Rebecca Harris leads a Commons debate on housing targets and Castle Point's Green Belt. A government minister normally replies.
body: Castle Point's MP, Dame Rebecca Harris, leads an adjournment debate in the House of Commons on Thursday 26 November. Her subject is housing targets and protecting Green Belt land on the edges of Benfleet, Canvey Island, Hadleigh and Thundersley. It is listed in the Hansard Society's guide to the week's business in Parliament. Adjournment debates come at the end of the day's sitting, so no fixed time has been given.
## Why it matters now

The debate follows the finding by government-appointed inspectors that the Castle Point Plan is unsound as the council submitted it, [as The Seax reported on 3 November](/story/castle-point-plan-unsound-inspectors/). The plan runs from 2026 to 2043 and proposes 6,196 homes. The government's standard method figure for the borough is 11,662. The inspectors want Castle Point Borough Council to look again at Green Belt sites that could bring its total closer to that number.

The council's current leaders chose to build mainly on brownfield land, rather than follow the previous administration's 2022 plan, which proposed large Green Belt releases. Deputy leader Councillor Warren Gibson has pointed to the borough's Green Belt, wildlife sites, congested roads and stretched services. The council said it would seek further advice on its next steps.
## The MP's position

Dame Rebecca, a Conservative, spoke at the inspectors' first hearings in September. She has opposed Green Belt housing schemes in the constituency, including North Benfleet Hall Farm and up to 165 homes at Glebelands, and has objected to the council's grey belt classification.
## What happens next
A minister usually answers for the government at the end of an adjournment debate. The Seax will report what was said, and the government's reply, once the official Hansard record is published.
points: Inspectors found the Castle Point Plan unsound in early November
The plan proposes 6,196 homes against a government figure of 11,662
The council has not yet said how it will respond
stories.newAngle: Castle Point's MP takes the borough's Green Belt and housing target dispute to a Commons debate on 26 November.

stories.headline: Air ambulance charity to study how to cut Essex road deaths
stories.summary: Essex & Herts Air Ambulance will study Essex crash data to learn how more lives could be saved. Road safety money is paying for it.
body: Essex & Herts Air Ambulance has won funding from the Safer Essex Roads Partnership to find out what more could be done to stop people dying on the county's roads. Your Harlow reported the grant on Thursday 26 November. The money comes from the partnership's Road Safety Intervention Funding.
## What the research will look at

The charity will go through road crash records with the police, the highways authority and the fire and rescue service, starting with five years of figures. Researchers will look at the injuries people suffered and when they got medical help. The aim is to see whether new or faster treatment could change the outcome for future patients.
It builds on work the charity already does. After every death on one of its missions, its team reviews the case with a forensic pathologist.
## Who is involved

Dr Gareth Grier, the charity's associate medical director, leads its Centre for Excellence, which will oversee the project. An academic research fellow is being recruited to run it. “We know that dispatching an air ambulance can save vital minutes,” Dr Grier said.

Roger Hirst, Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner for Essex, chairs the partnership's governance board. He said every minute counts when a serious incident happens. Volunteers from the charity's patient and public involvement group, including bereaved families, will help shape the work.
## The bigger goal

The partnership launched its Vision Zero strategy in November 2020. It aims for no deaths or serious injuries on roads in Essex, Southend and Thurrock by 2040, and to halve them by 2030. At the launch, the air ambulance charity said 42 people had died on Essex roads in 2019. The charity has not said when the research will report its findings.
points: Five years of crash data will be studied first
A research fellow is being recruited to lead it
Bereaved families will help shape the work

stories.headline: Witham bus link to Broomfield Hospital starts year-long trial
stories.summary: Witham patients and visitors get a direct bus to Broomfield Hospital from Monday 30 November. It runs on demand for a 12-month trial.
body: Witham people will be able to book a direct bus to Broomfield Hospital from Monday 30 November, after years of campaigning, the Braintree and Witham Times reported. The service is run by DigiGo, Essex County Council's on-demand minibus scheme, and starts as a one-year trial.

Witham Town Council won £50,000 for the link from Essex County Council's Love Your Bus grant fund. Braintree District Council is adding £30,000 of Section 106 money, paid by developers to fund local services. The town council thanked the local groups, residents and councillors who gave evidence for the bid.
## How it will work

According to the town council's September newsletter, the bus runs Monday to Friday, with up to four return journeys a day. There is no fixed timetable. Passengers book a trip in advance or on demand through the TravelEssex app or a telephone booking line, and can pay and track the bus in the app. Virtual pick-up and drop-off points across Witham link straight to the hospital.
Holders of a concessionary bus pass travel free after 9am. The town council has not published other fares, and the full list of pick-up points was not available when The Seax checked.
## What happens next

The trial lasts 12 months. Witham Town Council says the service could carry on after that if it becomes self-funding, so how many people use it will decide its future. Details are on the town council's Broomfield bus link page and at digigo.uk.
points: Funded by £50,000 from Love Your Bus and £30,000 from Braintree District Council
Book through the TravelEssex app or by phone
Free for bus pass holders after 9am

stories.headline: Stanway roundabout works bring more road closures into December
stories.summary: Closures for the new Fiveways roundabout in Stanway run into December. Peartree Road and London Road are next.
body: Drivers in Stanway face more closures in the run-up to Christmas as work on the new Fiveways roundabout goes on. Stanway Parish Council's roadworks list, updated on Friday 20 November, shows closures on Dyers Road and Heath Road that began in mid-November and run for 33 days each.

The Daily Gazette reported residents' confusion over the closures and warnings about restricted access. The parish council lists the orders under the Road Traffic Regulation Act and says they are needed for the safety of the public and the workforce.
## What is being built

Natta Building Company, working for Mersea Homes and Hills Residential, is building a four-arm roundabout at the Fiveways junction. Essex Highways says it is part of the Mersea Homes development at Fiveways Fruit Farm, where 420 homes won consent in 2021. Laurence Byrne Avenue will be extended from Warren Lane to Fiveways. The aim is to take pressure off Blackberry Road by letting traffic use the Tollgate relief road. Main works began in January and were expected to take about a year.
## Dates to know

London Road closes for two nights from Monday 30 November, 7pm to 5am, for carriageway patching by Essex County Council. Peartree Road closes for four days from 4 December for the junction work. Essex Highways says closures are used only when essential and come with signed diversions. Questions go to Natta on 01252 851155.
points: Dyers Road and Heath Road orders each run for 33 days
Work is linked to 420 homes at Fiveways Fruit Farm
Natta can be reached on 01252 851155

stories.headline: Tube strike: Essex commuters face late start and disrupted lines until midday
stories.summary: Central line passengers from Epping, Loughton and Buckhurst Hill face a disrupted journey. Transport for London expects a normal service by early evening.
body: Tube trains start late on Friday 27 November, from about 7am, and every line is disrupted until the RMT drivers' 24-hour walkout ends at 11.59am. No trains ran anywhere on the London Underground from 9pm on Thursday 26 November, after last-ditch talks at the conciliation service Acas ended without a deal.
Services run on all lines after midday, but Transport for London does not expect a normal service until about 6pm.

For Essex, the line that matters most is the Central line, which runs out to Buckhurst Hill, Loughton, Debden, Theydon Bois and Epping. Passengers using it on Friday morning should expect a late first train and disruption until midday, and allow extra time for the journey home.

The Piccadilly, Circle and Waterloo & City lines stay shut until the walkout is over. Travellers heading from Essex to Heathrow can use the Elizabeth line instead, which runs direct from Shenfield, Brentwood and Romford.
## What is still running

TfL says the Elizabeth line, DLR, London Overground, buses and trams will run as normal, but will be busier than usual. Greater Anglia and c2c trains into Liverpool Street and Fenchurch Street are not part of the strike, though passengers changing onto the Tube at either end will be affected.
## Why drivers are striking

The row is over plans to move Tube drivers from a five-day to a four-day week. The RMT says drivers would have to give up existing protections whether they chose four days or five, and that those who refused could be moved away from their depots. Aslef, the other drivers' union, supports the four-day week.

TfL told the BBC it had promised during the talks to work on proposals covering several of the union's concerns, and had asked the RMT to postpone the strike while it did so. The union refused. Acas says it remains in contact with both sides.

This is the first of eight strikes. The others are planned for 17 and 19 December, 4 and 6 January, and 17, 23 and 25 February. TfL is asking passengers to check before they travel and allow extra time.
points: Elizabeth line, DLR, Overground and buses unaffected
First of eight walkouts over the winter
Next strikes on 17 and 19 December

stories.headline: Chelmsford gets Lifted as Lighthouse Family's Tunde hits the High Street
stories.summary: Tunde Baiyewu marked his 58th birthday with a surprise lunchtime gig. Choir singers posing as shoppers joined in.
body: Lunchtime shoppers on Chelmsford High Street thought they were watching an ordinary busker on Wednesday 25 November. Singer Amber Prothero started Ocean Drive, the title track of Lighthouse Family's 1995 debut album, with a guitarist and choir leader Howard Francis beside her.
Then Tunde himself appeared and took over the song he made famous.

The pair went straight into High, the duo's biggest hit. It reached number four in the UK in 1998 and went to number one in Australia. By now a crowd was building, and many of the people in it were not who they seemed.
## The secret choir

The gig was organised by The BIG Sing, a community choir with groups across Essex. Members were told to come in their everyday clothes and stand "casually scattered around the High Street, looking like ordinary shoppers". They were asked not to bunch together, but to stop, watch and drift into the crowd like curious passers-by.
Singers were also told not to post about it or tell anyone outside the choir. The surprise was the whole point.
The reveal came on the third song. As Tunde started Rain To A Rainbow, a song from his solo work, the "shoppers" around him began to sing.

They stayed with him for the rest of the six-song set. Next came Bill Withers' Lean On Me, then (I Wish I Knew How It Would Feel to Be) Free / One, which went to number six in 2001. He finished with Lifted, the song that made Lighthouse Family's name.
Singer Rox Creeve also sang with him. Afterwards she posted a selfie with the star on Instagram, calling him "the absolute legend" and wishing him a happy birthday.
The Chelmsford For You page, which shared a video of the gig, said it had "not been your average hump day" in the city centre.

Each singer paid £10 towards the costs. A professional crew filmed the performance, and the organisers plan to share the footage on social media and send it to the national press in the hope it goes viral.
## The voice of Lighthouse Family

Tunde was born in London and grew up partly in Nigeria. He met keyboard player Paul Tucker while studying in Newcastle, and they formed Lighthouse Family in 1993. Ocean Drive went six times platinum in the UK, and the duo's albums have sold more than 15 million copies worldwide.

He already had links with the choir. In March he was billed as special guest at The BIG Sing's concert at Charter Hall in Colchester. That show had a 450-voice choir from Essex, Kent and the Midlands, including more than 100 Essex schoolchildren.
## The BIG Sing

Husband and wife Howard and Gemma Francis started The BIG Sing. Both used to sing with the London Community Gospel Choir. Howard, a keyboard player and songwriter, has toured with Westlife and Will Young and was musical director for Mis-Teeq.

The choir won over the judges on Britain's Got Talent in 2023 and won the Pride of Essex Award in 2017. It says it has raised more than £200,000 for good causes. Its Chelmsford choir rehearses on Wednesday evenings at Writtle Christian Centre, and money raised goes to its own charity, SOUL.
## See him again

Fans who missed the High Street gig will not have long to wait. Lighthouse Family are back on tour next year with Ocean Drive Live, celebrating their first album. The nearest dates are the London Palladium on 15 March and 6 April, and the Regent Theatre in Ipswich on 12 April.
points: Six songs, from Ocean Drive to Lifted
The choir revealed itself on the third song
Lighthouse Family play Ipswich on 12 April

stories.headline: M25 delays ease after crash just past A127 junction near Upminster
stories.summary: A collision at about 6.45pm held traffic heading for Thurrock. Queues had cleared by about 7.25pm.

also.name: National Highways live traffic data (via UK Traffic Updates)

body: Delays on the M25 clockwise near Upminster had eased by about 7.25pm. National Highways' live traffic data no longer showed queues between junctions 28 and 30, about 40 minutes after a collision brought traffic to a stop.

All traffic was held on the clockwise side just after junction 29, where the M25 meets the A127, after the collision. Essex County Council's Essex Travel News reported it at 6.45pm and warned that delays were building.

National Highways' live traffic data showed queues on the clockwise side between junction 28, for the A12 at Brook Street, and junction 30 for the A13 at Thurrock, from 6.43pm. At first it put the delays at 10 to 20 minutes.
There is no word on whether anyone was hurt. Essex Police had not posted about the crash by 7.25pm.
Separately, National Highways had already planned to shut the M25 clockwise between junctions 29 and 30 overnight, from 10pm until 5.30am, for roadworks.
