stories.headline: Report warns worker shortage could delay Lower Thames Crossing and pylons
stories.summary: Two of the East's biggest schemes are in Essex. Their busiest years clash with other projects, and too few local people are being trained.
body: A shortage of skilled workers could push up costs and delay major building projects across the East of England, including two in Essex, a report by MPs and council leaders warns.

[Opportunity East: Closing the Infrastructure Skills Gap](https://www.localgoveasteng.gov.uk/content/uploads/2026/11/Opportunity-East-Closing-the-Infrastructure-Skills-Gap-November-2026.pdf) was launched at the House of Lords on Tuesday by Local Government East and the East of England All-Party Parliamentary Group. It says the region has 57 Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects, more than any other part of the country.

Government figures suggest up to 30,080 workers will be needed to build them over the next five years, the report says. Many of the projects will be at their busiest between 2028 and 2030, and they need the same trades: civil engineers, electricians, steel fixers, plant operators and quantity surveyors.
## The Essex projects

The Lower Thames Crossing, the new road and tunnel under the Thames between Thurrock and Kent, will need about 3,000 workers at its peak, according to the report. National Highways started early work in Essex and Kent in March.
National Highways aims to recruit at least 45% of the crossing's workforce from within 20 miles. It wants 20% from the communities closest to the route, including Thurrock and Brentwood.

National Grid's Norwich to Tilbury power line would need 1,720 workers at its peak. Planning inspectors had sent their recommendation on the line, about 180km long, to the energy secretary by 10 November. A decision is expected within three months.

The report says the crossing, the power line and the Sealink power cable will all be at their busiest around 2028 to 2030. At the same time, Sizewell C in Suffolk and the Universal theme park in Bedfordshire will still be building up their workforces.

It lists Stansted Airport's expansion among the region's major projects. It also says the Harlow and Gilston Garden Town will bring a further 23,000 homes in Essex and Hertfordshire, needing many of the same skills.
## Young people left out
Around 90,000 people aged 16 to 24 in the East were not in education, employment or training at the end of 2025, the report says. That is 11.7% of the age group.

Among 16 and 17-year-olds, the Essex County Council area does worse than the national average. [Department for Education figures](https://explore-education-statistics.service.gov.uk/find-statistics/participation-in-education-training-and-neet-age-16-to-17-by-local-authority/2025-26) show 6.2% of that age group there were not in education, employment or training, or their activity was not known.
That compares with 5.8% across England and 4.9% across the East. The rate was 5.1% in Southend and 3.8% in Thurrock. The figures are an average of December 2025 to February 2026.
## What the report wants
Its main call is for the government to back a single workforce plan for the region's infrastructure, so colleges and training providers can see which jobs are needed, how many, where and when.

It also wants skills money handed to the region sooner, ahead of mayoral elections. Greater Essex's first mayoral election was due in May 2026 but [has been put back to May 2028](https://www.colchester.gov.uk/elections/postponed-elections).

Other recommendations include requiring big infrastructure projects to commit to hiring young people, as Alan Milburn's recent report on young people proposed. It also wants better transport so people can reach training and jobs, and says adult skills funding has fallen by 25% in real terms over ten years.
## Training in Essex

The report holds up the region's Clean Energy Technical Excellence College, run by Colchester Institute, as the kind of joined-up working that is needed. But it says funding for such schemes needs to improve.
Colchester Institute won that status in April. The college said then that up to 60,000 clean energy jobs are expected in the East by 2030.
## What they said

Councillor Carl Smith, chair of Local Government East and leader of Great Yarmouth Borough Council, said: "Unless we invest now in skills, training and workforce planning, we risk missing a once-in-a-generation opportunity."

Jess Asato, the Labour MP for Lowestoft and co-chair of the parliamentary group, said the report tackled "one of the most important challenges facing our region and the country: matching jobs to people".
The growth minister, Dan Tomlinson, called the report "timely". He told the launch: "I have read your report and I will direct my civil servants to come and talk to you."
points: The report wants one workforce plan and skills money handed to the region sooner
Lower Thames Crossing needs about 3,000 at its peak, the Norwich to Tilbury line 1,720
6.2% of 16 and 17-year-olds in the Essex County Council area are NEET or not known, above England's 5.8%

stories.headline: Southend: four masked men attack man who refused to hand over money
stories.summary: A man in his 30s was left with rib and neck injuries. Police want to hear from anyone who saw what happened.
body: A man was attacked by four men in Clifftown Road, Southend, after he refused to give them money, Essex Police said.
The man, who is in his 30s, was left with injuries to his ribs and neck. It happened at about 8.30pm on Tuesday 24 November, and police are treating it as a robbery.
The four men were dressed all in black and wore balaclavas.
Officers believe other people were in the area at the time and may have seen what happened. They want to hear from anyone with information, or with CCTV, dash cam or other footage.

Anyone who can help should quote crime reference 42/187896/26. Reports can be made on the Essex Police website or through its online Live Chat, which runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week. To stay anonymous, contact the independent charity Crimestoppers online or on 0800 555 111.

stories.headline: Southend shoplifter jailed for stealing from shop he was banned from
stories.summary: Josh Love, 31, stole from the One Stop in Sutton Road five times in five days despite a court ban.
body: A Southend shoplifter who was banned from a city shop by the courts has been jailed for 48 weeks after stealing from it five times in five days, Essex Police said.

Josh Love, 31, had been barred from entering the One Stop Shop in Sutton Road for two years under a criminal behaviour order imposed in January, the Gazette reported. Breaking such an order is a criminal offence in its own right.
Southend magistrates heard he ignored the ban. He admitted 16 counts of shop theft committed between 1 and 18 November.
As well as the One Stop Shop, he stole groceries from Tesco and Sainsbury's in Southchurch Road. The goods he took were worth more than £1,600 in total.
points: Jailed for 48 weeks by Southend magistrates
16 shop thefts between 1 and 18 November
More than £1,600 of goods taken

stories.headline: Tendring keeps second homes council tax premium for another year
stories.summary: Second home owners in Tendring will keep paying double council tax from April. Help for struggling working-age households could also be backdated.
body: Tendring District Council has agreed to keep its council tax discounts and extra charges unchanged for 2027/28, including the 100 per cent premium on second homes. Full Council made the decision on Tuesday 24 November, and the arrangements start on 1 April 2027.

Owners of long-term empty properties will also keep paying extra charges at today's levels, and the existing exceptions stay in place. Care leavers moving towards independent living will still get help with their bills. Cabinet has widened the council's hardship policy so it can consider cases involving the extra charges on second homes and empty properties.

Council leader Councillor Mark Stephenson said the number of second homes in Tendring fell by 186 in the past year. He said the premium was about bringing properties into use as permanent homes, "not raising more council tax".
## Backdated help for working-age claimants

Councillor Stephenson has also backed plans for working-age residents to have Local Council Tax Support claims backdated by up to three months, [as The Seax reported last week](/story/cw-tendring-council-tax-support-backdating-working-age/). Pension-age claimants can already do this. Eligible working-age residents get up to 80 per cent off their bills, and that level would stay the same next year. Claimants would need to show they qualified during the backdated period.

"When residents are struggling, a little help at the right time can stop things getting worse," he said. The backdating plan is still subject to consultation. A draft scheme goes to the council's cabinet in December, with a final decision expected in January 2027.
points: New arrangements start on 1 April 2027
Working-age support stays at up to 80% off bills
Final decision on backdating due in January 2027
stories.newAngle: Full Council on 24 November kept the discounts and the second homes premium unchanged for 2027/28.

stories.headline: Essex Poundland stores stay open for now as chain falls into administration
stories.summary: Poundland's shops across Essex are still trading after the chain collapsed. Administrators are now looking for a buyer.
body: Poundland went into administration on Wednesday 25 November, putting its shops in Essex towns including Southend, Chelmsford and Colchester at risk. The Press Association reported that specialists from the corporate finance firm AlixPartners have been appointed as administrators.

For now nothing changes for shoppers. The retailer will keep trading from its stores while the administrators search for a buyer, and no closures have been announced. Around 600 stores and some 11,000 jobs across the UK are at risk.
## How it got here

Gordon Brothers bought Poundland for £1 last year and began a sale process in September. Poundland first filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators on 29 October, which gave it 10 working days of protection from creditors. It filed a second notice on 12 November after the first expired, ITV News reported. MPs had accused the owner of cutting off funding.

Several bids fell through, including offers from Martin Property Group, Xyra Holdings and Zachert Private Equity. Tesco, Iceland and Lidl had been in talks over some of the shops. More than 100 Poundland stores had already shut during the owner's turnaround.
## What happens next

AlixPartners said it was "a deeply concerning time for all involved". The administrators will now try to sell all or part of the business. The Seax will report any decisions on individual Essex stores when they are announced.
points: AlixPartners appointed as administrators
Gordon Brothers bought the chain for £1
No store closures announced yet

stories.headline: Gilston's first 276 homes by Harlow: what the new village will include
stories.summary: Plans for the first homes in the Gilston expansion next to Harlow are now approved. Here is what the new village will include.
body: The first 276 homes in Village 7 of the Gilston Area, just north of Harlow across the River Stort, have detailed planning approval from East Herts Council. Savills, which handled the application for the builder, announced the approval on 29 October. The Harlow and Gilston Garden Town partnership set out on Wednesday 25 November what the village will include.

Of the 276 homes, 65 are affordable: 39 for affordable rent and 26 for shared ownership, in a mix of one to five bedrooms. Taylor Wimpey is building the village, which East Herts Council says will have 1,500 homes in all. Every home will be linked to a shared heating and hot water network, and the Community Heat Hub behind it must be working before the first residents move in.
## What the village will have

Walking and cycling routes will run separately through Church Lane Green, with links to a planned public transport corridor and more than 1,000 cycle parking spaces. Residents will get raised beds for growing food, a foraging trail of fruit plants, a sensory garden and a farm-themed play area, plus five smaller play spots along everyday routes. The village masterplan, approved in April, also includes a football hub and the restoration of listed barns for offices and community use.

Councillor Maura Connolly, East Herts Council's executive member for planning and growth, called it "a major moment for Gilston". Jonathan Locke, head of planning at Taylor Wimpey North Thames, said work could now start on what will become the gateway to the new community.
## Why it matters for Harlow

Gilston sits in Hertfordshire, but the garden town brings it together with Harlow's plans for homes, jobs and transport on both sides of the county border. [Planners heard last week that the whole Gilston scheme is a 30-year job](/story/o-gilston-area-10000-homes-30-year-vision-east-herts/), with schools, green space and other infrastructure to follow the homes.
points: Approval announced by Savills on 29 October
39 homes for affordable rent, 26 shared ownership
More than 1,000 cycle parking spaces planned
stories.newAngle: The first 276 homes in Village 7 now have detailed approval, and the garden town has set out what the village will include.

stories.headline: Brightlingsea councillors fight 550-home bid for Church Road land
stories.summary: Brightlingsea's councillors oppose a bid for 550 homes on the town's edge. They want the land kept out of Tendring's new Local Plan.
body: Brightlingsea's ward councillors have come out against a bid by Trinity College to have its land on the edge of the town included in Tendring District Council's updated Local Plan. Brightlingsea Town Council set out their opposition in a statement on Wednesday 25 November.
The college owns land on both sides of Church Road. It has put forward detailed plans to use a wider area there for 550 homes, the town council says.
## How we got here

Earlier this year the college's first proposal, for 300 homes, was taken out of the draft plan after local opposition. Tendring District Council said in June that it would remove the proposal for 300 homes on land east of Church Road after significant public objections and concerns raised by the town council. It said it would look instead at spreading growth across a number of smaller sites.

The Local Plan decides where new homes go across the district. Tendring must plan for 18,000 new homes up to 2043, after government targets almost doubled its yearly requirement from 550 homes to nearly 1,070.
## What councillors say

Councillor Jayne Chapman raised the issue at the district council's Planning Policy and Local Plan Committee on 17 November. Councillor Mick Barry spoke against the plans at the full Tendring council meeting the following Tuesday, 24 November.
## What happens next

The ward councillors say they will coordinate a response from the town council and community groups to back the district council's planning officers in opposing the land's inclusion. They plan to ask for more information and hold meetings in the town to gather local knowledge. That will feed into submissions to the independent planning inspector, whose hearings are expected in 2027.
points: First proposal for 300 homes was removed from the draft plan
Tendring must plan for 18,000 homes up to 2043
Inspector's hearings expected in 2027

stories.headline: Southchurch Library: 2,600 have their say as four options stay open
stories.summary: More than 2,600 people took part in Southend City Council's review of Southchurch Library. No decision has been made on its future.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council said on Wednesday 25 November that more than 2,600 people took part in its review of Southchurch Library. The consultation ran from 28 August to 8 October and drew 712 formal responses, as well as visitors to a series of drop-in sessions around Southchurch.

The library has been in trouble for years. It moved into its current building in 1972 as a temporary home after leaving Southchurch Hall. That building is a prefabricated timber structure that was expected to last about 25 years. More than 50 years on, the council says it has been assessed as being in very poor condition and needs significant investment.
## The four options

Four choices are still on the table: refurbishing the existing building, a new build on the same site, moving the library into Southend City Community College, or finding another location in the Southchurch area. The council puts the likely costs at between about £150,000 for relocation and about £750,000 for alternative provision. It has not published a figure for each option.
Most people who responded wanted to keep a library on the current site. They spoke about how easy it is to reach and its value as a place for the community.

Councillor Matt Dent, cabinet member for business, culture, music and tourism, said "the level of engagement has been extremely strong". Councillor Kevin Robinson, cabinet member for planning, property and governance, stressed that no decision has yet been made.
## What happens next

The council's Place Overview and Scrutiny Committee will look at the findings on 3 December. Councillors there will give feedback but will not be asked to choose a preferred option. Cabinet will then consider recommendations and decide the next steps on 17 December.
points: 712 formal responses to the consultation
Building opened in 1972 as a temporary home
Scrutiny committee meets on 3 December
Cabinet decides next steps on 17 December

stories.headline: Felsted School meets every standard in October inspection
stories.summary: Inspectors praised Felsted School's safeguarding culture and its curriculum for the youngest pupils.
body: Felsted School has met all of the Independent School Standards after an inspection in October 2026, according to the inspectors' report, which the school published in November.
The Independent Schools Inspectorate (ISI) carried out the visit. It is appointed by the Department for Education to inspect schools that belong to the independent school associations in England.

Inspectors looked at five areas: leadership, management and governance; the quality of education, training and recreation; physical and mental health and emotional wellbeing; social and economic education and contribution to society; and safeguarding. According to the school, they judged it to be meeting the required standards in all of them and commented positively on every part of its provision.

On safeguarding, the report describes a 'strong safeguarding culture where pupils feel safe and staff are well trained'. Inspectors called the curriculum for the youngest learners 'ambitious, coherent and responsive to children's interests'.

Felsted's head is Lara Pechard. Its earlier full ISI reports, from 2023 and 2019, sit on the school's website beside the new one. The Dunmow Broadcast first reported the outcome on Wednesday 25 November.
points: Inspection carried out by the Independent Schools Inspectorate in October 2026
Five areas checked, from leadership to pupils' wellbeing
Earlier full reports from 2023 and 2019 are also online

stories.headline: Clacton woman admits 14 shop thefts including Christmas selection boxes
stories.summary: Tayla Sabaroche, 27, took more than £2,100 of goods from shops in Clacton and Walton. She will be sentenced in February.
body: A Tendring woman has admitted stealing more than £2,100 of goods from shops in Clacton and Walton, Essex Police said.

Tayla Sabaroche, 27, of no fixed address, admitted 14 counts of shop theft before Basildon magistrates on Monday 23 November. She also admitted making off without paying for petrol at a garage in Manningtree.

The court heard she stole from Asda, Boots, Iceland, Morrisons and Tesco in Clacton, and the Co-op in Walton, between 5 September and 18 November. The goods included sweets, chocolates, toys, clothes and alcohol.
An officer from Clacton Local Policing Team arrested her in Kings Parade, Holland-on-Sea, on Sunday 22 November. She is due to be sentenced at Chelmsford Magistrates' Court on 15 February 2027.
points: Thefts between 5 September and 18 November
Also admitted a petrol drive-off in Manningtree
Arrested in Holland-on-Sea on 22 November

stories.headline: Thurrock says SEND support is safe as councillors scrutinise budget cuts
stories.summary: Thurrock's draft savings for 2027/28 have been before scrutiny councillors. The council insists SEND support will not be cut.
body: Thurrock councillors examined the council's draft savings for 2027/28 at the corporate overview and scrutiny committee on Tuesday 24 November. Your Thurrock reported on 25 November that the plans lean on cutting temporary accommodation costs through homelessness prevention, reforming adult social care and SEND transport, using more technology and getting more from council property. The council said it is not proposing any cut to SEND provision. The transport savings relate to taxi arrangements, not to children's education support.

Council leader Richard Bingley said the council "still faces significant financial challenges". He said new financial controls now cover procurement, property and community grants. Councillor Sara Poyntz, cabinet member for finance, called them "challenging decisions, but they are responsible decisions".
## What else is proposed

Two of the plans reach straight into residents' pockets and staff desks. Your Thurrock reported on 23 November that the first residents' parking permit would stay at £30, but a second would rise from £40 to £62 and a third from £50 to £72. A household with three permits would pay £164 a year instead of £120. Council papers say those who take up the most parking space should contribute the most. The change would start on 1 April 2027 and is forecast to raise about £50,000 a year. No consultation is planned, because the permit zones are covered by traffic regulation orders.

The council would also stop buying new mobile phones for staff. Checks found a significant number of handsets that were unused or had never been switched on. Instead it would recycle devices, move more calls to Microsoft Teams and offer willing staff an eSIM work number on their own phone. It spends about £20,000 a year on handsets, and the plan could save up to £25,000. A council spokesman said any use of personal phones would meet data protection rules. The Seax first reported both plans last week, on [parking permits](/story/thurrock-parking-permits-more-than-one-car-higher-charges/) and [staff phones](/story/thurrock-council-staff-mobile-phones-budget-savings/).
## Why the council is cutting

Thurrock is still recovering from failed investments that left it deep in debt. According to the council, a quarter of its yearly revenue budget goes on debt linked to those investments. It still needs more than £60m of exceptional financial support from the government. Councillor Sara Poyntz, cabinet member for finance, said: "I want to be clear that these are just proposals at this stage." She added that residents would be consulted on the plans.
## What happens next

Scrutiny councillors can make recommendations but cannot block the plans. The council says the proposals now move through the budget process, including a public consultation, and the full council will consider the 2027/28 budget in February 2027. Even if the permit rises survive that process, they would need a separate decision before they start.
points: Second car permit would go from £40 to £62
SEND savings cover taxi transport, not education support
Full council sets the 2027/28 budget in February
stories.newAngle: The savings proposals, including the permit rises and the end of staff phone purchases, go before Thurrock's corporate overview and scrutiny committee on Tuesday 24 November.

stories.headline: Thurrock records Essex's highest level of fire incidents, report finds
stories.summary: Deliberate fires rose across Thurrock last year. A council safety report names arson as an emerging risk.
body: Your Thurrock reported on Wednesday 25 November that the Thurrock Community Safety Partnership's 2025/26 annual report puts the borough top in Essex for fire incidents. It names deliberate fire-setting and arson-related antisocial behaviour as risks needing more action.

Overall recorded crime fell slightly, and domestic abuse incidents dropped by 11.6%. The partnership ran on £41,905 last year. Councillors discuss the findings at the Place Overview and Scrutiny Committee on Thursday.
points: Domestic abuse incidents fell 11.6%
Partnership budget was £41,905, with no direct council cash
Grays Riverside named an antisocial behaviour hotspot
stories.researchNote: Searched for the Community Safety Partnership report and other coverage; Yellow Advertiser's report refused automated reading and the committee papers did not appear in results. Research again next run.

body: Baroness Taylor of Stevenage, the housing and local government minister, gave the government's verdict on Wednesday 25 November. Her letter replies to the seventh report from the commissioners sent in to run parts of Thurrock Council. She agreed with their finding that the council is far stronger than when the government intervened, with the clearest gains in leadership, governance, financial management and grip on the organisation.

Her letter, published on GOV.UK, warns that recovery is not yet secured. Thurrock must set and deliver a balanced budget for 2027/28, backed by a pipeline of savings that recur year after year. It must keep paying down its debt and finish rewriting its constitution, its financial procedure rules and its scheme of delegation. She also wants the council's change programme to move to what she calls "disciplined delivery, clear accountability" and measurable results.

Commissioners Gavin Jones and Denise Murray proposed an assurance plan setting out the evidence needed before the government steps back any further, and the minister backed it. It will set measures and milestones that give the council and ministers a shared route to ending the intervention. She also decided not to appoint a third commissioner for now, though that stays under review. The commissioners' next report is due in the spring and will help decide the intervention's future.

Thurrock's finances collapsed in 2022, and selling land and buildings is part of its recovery plan. The council has a £104.1m target for asset sales over five years. Four more council plots in Tilbury are proposed for sale, including nine acres north of Parker Avenue, [as The Seax reported on 13 November](/story/tilbury-four-council-land-plots-sale-objections/). Objections can be lodged until 5pm on Friday 27 November.

The council has other deadlines too. Earlier this month the Department for Education told Thurrock to rewrite its special educational needs strategy before help with its deficit could be released, [as The Seax reported on 7 November](/story/thurrock-send-strategy-deferred/). In January, answering the sixth report, ministers let Thurrock recruit its own chief executive, Local Government Lawyer reported.
stories.headline: Thurrock Council 'substantially stronger' but not yet fixed, minister says
points: No third commissioner will be appointed for now
Next commissioners' report is due in spring 2027
Objections to the Tilbury land sales close at 5pm on 27 November
stories.summary: A minister says Thurrock Council has improved greatly since commissioners were sent in during 2022. But its finances remain a major challenge.

stories.headline: Southend City Council urges Direct Debit sign-ups for £100 energy payment
stories.summary: Households who already pay council tax this way will get the government's new payment automatically. Others will have to ask for it.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council on Wednesday 25 November asked residents to switch their council tax to Direct Debit, so the government's one-off £100 Household Energy Payment reaches them automatically when payments begin in January.

Anyone already paying that way will see the money go straight into their bank account, with no form to fill in. People who pay another way will be invited by the council to apply, and the council says more details will follow. You can set up a Direct Debit online at southend.gov.uk/CtaxOnline.
Council leader Daniel Cowan said there would be "no need to apply" for Direct Debit users.
## Why it matters this winter

The payment arrives as household bills climb. The energy price cap rises by 26% to £2,166 a year in January, [as The Seax reported on Wednesday](/story/essex-energy-bills-price-cap-rise-26-percent-january-2027/). The £100 is aimed at homes in council tax bands A to D, and in Basildon alone about 65,000 homes fall in those bands, [The Seax found earlier this week](/story/basildon-100-household-energy-payment-65000-homes-bands-a-d/).
Southend's council has not said how many of its own households qualify or the exact date the money will land.
## Other help

Southend's cost of living pages at southend.gov.uk/costofliving set out other support, including Universal Credit, Pension Credit, Council Tax Reduction and local welfare assistance. A printed booklet with the same advice is available from the Civic Centre, libraries and partner organisations.
points: Payments start in January 2027
Non Direct Debit payers will be invited to apply
Cost of living booklet at libraries and the Civic Centre
stories.newAngle: Southend-on-Sea City Council told its own residents on 25 November that Direct Debit payers will be paid automatically and others must apply.

stories.headline: Brightlingsea promenade at Splash Point to reopen before Christmas
stories.summary: Brightlingsea's seafront path by the paddling pool is being resurfaced. The first stretch should be open again by Christmas.
body: Tendring District Council said on Wednesday 25 November that the first phase of work on the promenade around the paddling pool at Splash Point in Brightlingsea is nearly finished. The new surface is meant to make the seafront path easier to use, deal with years of wear and tear and drain better when it rains.

There will be limited or no access around Splash Point during the week starting Monday 30 November, while workers join the new surface to the existing stretch of promenade. Weather permitting, the council expects the first section to be fully open before Christmas. Councillor Adrian Smith, the cabinet member whose brief covers coast protection, said the aim was to have it "fully accessible before Christmas".

The project has taken longer than first planned. When Tendring District Council announced it in September, it said work would start in October and finish in November. The plan was to resurface whole sections rather than patch holes, with the path sloping gently from the sea wall towards the beach and raised slightly to make it easier for people with mobility problems.
## What happens next

The rest of the work has to fit around the tides, and there are no suitable working tides in January. The second phase is due to start in the first week of February 2027, with work on alternate weeks and a break for the Easter holidays. The council says it needs about five to six working weeks in total. Councillor Mick Barry, cabinet member for leisure and public realm, said he was pleased the council had secured the money for the work; the council has not said how much it costs.
points: Limited or no access at Splash Point from Monday 30 November
Phase two starts in the first week of February 2027
About five to six working weeks still needed, around the tides

stories.headline: Stansted Airport College to double in size with £5m from Essex council
stories.summary: Essex County Council's leader has set out why the county is backing the airport's college. He says Stansted is vital to jobs across Greater Essex.
body: Councillor Peter Harris, the leader of Essex County Council, used a guest blog published by London Stansted Airport on Wednesday 25 November to set out the council's £5m investment in Stansted Airport College. He said the money will more than double the college's capacity, giving more young people from across Greater Essex the chance to train for careers in aviation, engineering and aircraft maintenance.

Councillor Harris described the airport as "a vital piece of economic infrastructure". He pointed to its place as the largest single-site employer in Greater Essex and the East of England, with more than 12,000 people working there directly. He said the Greater Essex economy is worth £55 billion a year, and could produce up to £8 billion more each year if it matched productivity across the wider South East.

The blog follows the Greater Essex Government Showcase in Westminster last month, where council and business leaders made the case for investment in the area. Councillor Harris said continued investment in international links would bring in new business and better-paid jobs.
points: More than 12,000 people work at the airport directly
Greater Essex economy worth £55bn a year, says the council leader
Blog is part of the airport's guest series on connectivity

stories.headline: Harlow College students make consent films for 16 Days of Activism
stories.summary: Media students in Harlow have made four short films on consent and abusive relationships. Essex Sexual Health Service will share them online.
body: The videos, made by Harlow College's media and journalism students for a real brief, will run on Essex Sexual Health Service's social media and website from Wednesday 25 November to Thursday 10 December. Those dates mark the global 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence.

The students pitched their own ideas before filming. The films look at the online 'manosphere' and its view of masculinity, the warning signs of domestic abuse, coercive control, and consent and peer pressure. Sophie Milner, head of outreach and education at the service, said involving young people keeps the messages 'relevant, relatable and meaningful'.
points: Campaign runs until Thursday 10 December
Service run by Provide Community for Essex County Council
Advice and the films at eshs.org.uk

stories.headline: Saffron Walden to run free Christmas buses for two late-night events
stories.summary: Saffron Walden Town Council is laying on free buses for late shopping and its Christmas fayre.
body: The free hop-on, hop-off service will run from 4pm to 8pm on Friday 27 November and again on Friday 4 December, carrying people to and from the town centre. Saffron Walden Town Council announced the buses on 23 November, after its regular free Tuesday shopper bus finished for 2026.

The first date is the late-night shopping evening led by the town's Business Improvement District, when several shops stay open until 8pm. The second is the Walden Christmas Fayre and Lantern Parade, which the town council hosts with the Saffron Walden Initiative. Stalls and entertainment run from 2pm to 8pm, with carols in Market Square at 6pm.

Timings are flexible, and the council asks passengers to check with the driver when the bus reaches Market Square. Paper timetables are available from the Tourist Information Centre. The council has not published the routes or named the operator. The Saffron Walden Reporter also covered the service on 25 November.
points: Carols in Market Square at 6pm on 4 December
Paper timetables from the Tourist Information Centre
Routes and operator not yet published

stories.headline: Tendring to remove 55 recycling banks after kerbside glass rounds begin
stories.summary: Bottle banks across Tendring are going. Homes can now put glass out with their recycling instead.
body: Tendring District Council will take away all 55 of the recycling banks it runs across the district during December and January. The council announced the change on Wednesday 25 November, saying the banks are no longer needed now that glass, cartons and more plastics are collected from people's homes.

Since October, households have been able to put glass bottles and jars, Tetra Pak cartons and extra types of plastic out with their regular kerbside recycling. The rounds are run by the council's contractor, Veolia. Council figures show 281.4 tonnes of glass was collected in October, from the kerbside and the banks together. That compares with 165.8 tonnes in September, a rise of about 70%.

Doorstep glass collections began after [the council sent out 70,000 extra recycling boxes](/story/cw-tendring-glass-joins-kerbside-recycling-boxes/), and the first month's rounds were [covered by The Seax earlier this month](/story/o-tendring-glass-recycling-first-month-200-tonnes/).

Councillor Adrian Smith, cabinet member for environment, said people across Tendring had been doing "a fantastic job in recycling" and had stopped using the bottle banks. He said the council will not renew the contract to provide them, a decision he said "provides best value for the taxpayer". He also hopes it will cut fly-tipping, because rubbish is often dumped beside the banks.
## What happens next

Where a town or village has more than one bank, they will be taken away in stages, so people still using them have time to adjust. Posters have gone up on the banks, and the council has written to the owners of the land where they stand. The council says the move follows the government's Simpler Recycling rules. Residents can check what goes in which container on the council's Rubbish and Recycling web page.
points: Banks go in stages through December and January
Glass, Tetra Pak cartons and more plastics collected from homes since October
Contract to run the banks will not be renewed
stories.newAngle: The council is now removing all 55 of its recycling banks in December and January because glass is collected at the kerbside.

stories.headline: From best in Britain to below standard: what's going wrong at c2c
stories.summary: c2c topped Britain's punctuality table last spring. This autumn, just over half its stops have been on time. We look at why.
body: For years, the line from Fenchurch Street to Shoeburyness was the railway other commuters envied. Last May, c2c was named the most punctual train company in Britain. This autumn its passengers have had a very different railway.

The Seax has gone through c2c's own published performance figures, its apologies to passengers, Network Rail's explanations, the letter MPs sent to rail bosses and the replies to the operator's latest video apology. Together they show how fast the service has fallen, and why.
## The numbers

c2c publishes its figures every four weeks. In the four weeks to Sunday 15 November, 53.5% of its trains reached each stop within a minute of the timetable. In the four weeks to 31 May, the figure was 79.4%.

The wider measure the industry now uses tells the same story. It counts stops reached within three minutes of the timetable. That fell from 92.5% in May to 76.4% in the latest period, so nearly one stop in four missed even that mark.

It is a long way from last spring. In the year to 31 March 2026, Network Rail's figures put c2c top of the national table. It reached 91.9% of stops within three minutes and cancelled 1.7% of trains, the lowest rate in the country.
In the four weeks to 17 October, c2c cancelled 4.5% of station calls against its own target of 1.6%. Its rolling annual average on the three-minute measure has slipped to 88.4%.
## What has gone wrong
There is no single cause. The line has been hit by one problem after another.

First, the weather. The summer's heat and lack of rain shrank the clay under long stretches of track in Essex, leaving it uneven. Network Rail said soil moisture was at its lowest since its records began in 2009. Speed limits were brought in, and from 25 August c2c journeys between London and Southend took up to eight minutes longer. The operator says these restrictions caused most of its late running in the autumn, and that a full recovery is unlikely until they are lifted.
Signalling failures have stopped trains again and again.
On 8 and 9 September, a signalling problem in the Grays area hit the evening and morning peaks.
On 8 October, a fault at Gas Factory Junction, between Barking and West Ham, led to 81 cancellations on its own.
On 4 November, a failure between Stanford-le-Hope and Grays halted trains and left commuters stranded at Stanford-le-Hope, East Tilbury, Tilbury and Grays.
On 19 November, a fault between Fenchurch Street and Barking disrupted every line into the evening, and West Ham was not served.

The biggest single blow came from a freight train. On 23 October, a GB Railfreight container train heading from London Gateway to the Midlands came off the track near Barking. Rail investigators say the 20th of its 39 wagons derailed at about 8mph. The BBC reported that 1.2km of track was badly damaged. Trains to Purfleet, Rainham and Dagenham Dock did not call again until 11 November. c2c does not run freight trains, but its passengers bore the brunt.
Then, on the evening of Monday 23 November, a fire on a train at Fenchurch Street blocked every c2c line, with disruption expected until 9pm. c2c has not yet said what caused it.
In its own report on the period to 17 October, c2c said it missed every passenger satisfaction target. It blamed the reduced timetables, its older Class 357 trains and cleanliness.
## What passengers and MPs say

On 4 November, MPs from both main parties and an independent wrote to c2c and Network Rail demanding a meeting in Parliament. The letter was organised by Thurrock's Labour MP, Jen Craft. The BBC named its signatories as Ms Craft, James Asser and Margaret Mullane (Labour), Bayo Alaba (Independent), and Richard Holden, Julia Lopez, Mark Francois and Rebecca Harris (Conservative).

The MPs listed overcrowded trains, persistent cancellations, long delays and poor replacement transport. They said passengers were facing extra costs to get to work, school and hospital appointments. They asked for a clear explanation and a date when a reliable service would return.

Ms Craft, who commutes on the line herself, told the BBC it had been "one thing after another" this year. She said the line was once known as the "misery line" in the 1990s, and she did not want it to go back to that. Incidents can happen, she said, but the response had been too slow and communication with passengers really poor.
Ms Craft said on 12 November that she had brought c2c and Network Rail's leaders to Parliament to press them. Neither side has published what was agreed.
## What c2c and Network Rail say

c2c has apologised many times this autumn. The most direct apology came at 3.23pm on Tuesday 24 November, in a video posted on c2c's X account. In it Jamie Burles, managing director of GBR Anglia, said the service over the past six months had not met the standards passengers rightly expect.
"Too many customers have experienced delays and cancellations," he said, adding that this had hurt confidence in the railway.

Mr Burles set out what is being done. Track teams are carrying out what he called unprecedented levels of treatment, to lift the temporary speed limits left by the hot, dry summer. GBR Anglia is also investing in the power supply: backup batteries, new critical power cables, better monitoring, overhead wires that cope better with heat, and specialist teams sent where they will help most.
Some of this will take time to finish, he said. "I know that words alone won't restore confidence," he added, promising to keep passengers updated.

Earlier in the month, Rob Mullen, chief customer and commercial officer for GBR Anglia, apologised after the 4 November failure. "We're really sorry that the service to passengers on the c2c network hasn't been good enough of late," he said. He said the team was working to restore services through Barking and to make the line more resilient, including to extreme weather.

Much of what has failed is not c2c's own. The track, signals and overhead wires belong to Network Rail, and the train that derailed belonged to a freight company. Network Rail says dried-out clay affects Greater Anglia, the Elizabeth line and lines in Kent and Sussex too.

But the line is now run as one. c2c has been publicly owned since July 2025. Since May 2026 it has been managed with Greater Anglia and Network Rail Anglia by a single leadership team, GBR Anglia, set up to bring track and train together. Mr Burles leads it. Ellie Burrows is managing director of Network Rail's Eastern region.
## 'It's a shambles': how passengers answered the apology
Passengers were quick to reply to Mr Burles' video on X. By the next morning it had been watched more than 50,000 times, and the replies show how far trust has fallen.

"I have lost all confidence in your trainline," wrote one commuter, posting as MrsLovingLife. "I, like many other commuters, wake up and think are we getting to work today? If we do, it's then, are we going to get home, hassle free? It's a shambles."

Kirsty MacDougall replied: "Oh the irony that I am watching this from yet another delayed train! That's three train journeys in a row now! C2C used to be such a reliable service. Hardly any issues. What happened!?"
Stuart A. wrote: "Sadly Apology not accepted. Excuses after excuses."

Others asked why the track work was not done during what Simon Lester called "the hottest summer for years". One passenger called for c2c to "drastically reduce fares until there's no more issues on the line". Another said they had not had a reply to a complaint made 96 days earlier. c2c answered, asking for the case reference so its customer relations team could chase it.
## What happens next

c2c says an elevated risk of cancellations is expected to last until February 2027. It says punctuality will not fully recover until the speed restrictions are lifted, and that this depends on the weather.
More engineering work is planned, including over the weekend of 28 and 29 November, so check before you travel.
If your journey is delayed by 15 minutes or more, you can claim compensation through c2c's Delay Repay scheme. c2c Smartcard holders are paid automatically for delays of more than two minutes.

A freight derailment, repeated signalling failures and dried-out clay all hit the line

body: The East of England Ambulance Service, which answers 999 calls across Essex, has been rated good by the Care Quality Commission. It comes 21 months after the regulator served it with a warning notice. The Cambridge Independent, BBC News and Suffolk News all reported the findings on Wednesday 25 November.

Its urgent and emergency care, the crews and ambulances that reach patients, has gone from inadequate to good. The emergency operations centres, where 999 calls are answered and crews sent out, have moved up from requires improvement. The trust as a whole is now rated good.

Both services were rated good in all five areas inspectors look at: whether care is safe, effective, caring, responsive and well led. The control rooms are no longer breaking the rules on safe care and staffing. Urgent and emergency care has met every demand in the warning notice.
## What inspectors found

Inspectors spent three days at the service in July. BBC News reported that they visited six ambulance stations and the control rooms in Bedford, Norwich and Chelmsford, and spoke to about 105 staff. They found quicker call handling and dispatch, better response times and more staff. Mandatory training, appraisals and safeguarding had all improved.

That came as the service got busier. The CQC found demand for ambulances in the region had risen by 19% since 2022. According to the BBC, most of the growth was in category 2 and 3 calls. Category 2 includes suspected strokes, seizures and burns. Category 3 covers less serious burns, women in late labour and people with diabetes.

Since its last inspection the trust has set up a Cardiac Arrest Desk. It puts 999 callers on a live video link to an advanced paramedic, who can talk them through CPR before the ambulance arrives. Inspectors said it was helping people get effective CPR sooner and supporting survival rates.
The BBC also reported that 90% of older people who call after a fall are now treated at the scene, compared with about 55% nationally. Compliments to the service outnumber complaints by nine to one.
## The problem that remains

The reports are not all good news. Ambulances are still being held in queues outside hospitals, and handover delays were rated the trust's highest operational risk. While a crew waits to hand over a patient, that ambulance cannot answer another 999 call. Suffolk News reported that response time targets for some patients were missed over the winter.
## How far the service has come

The regulator served the warning notice on 10 February 2025. It cited failings on staff training, staffing levels, call waiting times and the handling of controlled drug incidents. Its concerns also covered the culture of the service and how managers acted on staff feedback.

Problems had built up over several years. After inspections in April and May 2022, the CQC said ambulance response times were well below national standards. It also found staffing shortages that affected patient safety, and said not enough had been done to tackle a culture of bullying.
## What they said

Neill Moloney, the trust's chief executive, said the findings recognised 'the enormous amount of work' staff had put in. He said the trust still had to make sure leadership and management were consistently effective across urgent and emergency care.
Sarah Ivory Donnelly, the CQC's deputy director of hospitals in the East of England, said the trust 'should be happy with the improvements they've made'.

stories.headline: Essex energy bills to rise 26% in January as price cap hits £2,166
stories.summary: Homes across Essex on standard tariffs face dearer gas and electricity from New Year's Day. The regulator blames conflict in the Middle East.
body: Energy regulator Ofgem announced on Wednesday 25 November that its price cap will go up for the three months from 1 January to 31 March 2027. For a typical home using gas and electricity and paying by Direct Debit, the yearly figure rises from £1,723 to £2,166. That is £443 more.

The cap limits the unit rates and standing charges suppliers can set on default tariffs. It is not a ceiling on the total bill, so homes that use more energy pay more. Ofgem said about 20 million households on standard variable tariffs will be affected. About 10 million on fixed deals are protected until their deal ends.
## Why prices are going up

Ofgem said continued conflict in the Middle East is pushing up international gas prices. Neil Kenward, its director general for markets, said the conflict "continues to drive energy costs higher". Gas is rising faster than electricity, the regulator said, because more of Britain's power now comes from renewables rather than gas.
## Help with bills

Ofgem said the government will give about 20 million households £100 towards their energy bills from January. In Basildon alone, about 65,000 homes in council tax bands A to D are in line for that payment, [as The Seax reported on 21 November](/story/basildon-100-household-energy-payment-65000-homes-bands-a-d/).

Anyone struggling to pay should contact their supplier, which must offer support and advice, Ofgem said. It has written to suppliers asking them to spot people who need help early and to keep repayment plans affordable. Moving to Direct Debit saves the average customer about £160 a year, according to the regulator.
## What happens next

Ofgem reviews the cap every three months, so the next change will apply from 1 April 2027. Households on a standard tariff can also look at fixed deals, the regulator said, and the Energy Saving Trust gives advice on cutting energy use.
points: Applies from 1 January to 31 March 2027
About 20 million homes on standard tariffs affected
Fixed-deal customers protected until their deal ends
Direct Debit saves about £160 a year, Ofgem says

stories.headline: Fyfield field gives up rare 1646 Civil War siege coin
stories.summary: A detectorist has found a rare Civil War siege coin near Ongar. He fears he may not be allowed to keep it.
body: Lukasz Cedzidlo, of the Metal Detectives Group, found the coin in a field at Fyfield, near Ongar. It is stamped "OBS Newark" with the year, and his group believes it was made during the siege of Newark in the First English Civil War. BBC News reported the find on Wednesday 25 November.

Newark-on-Trent was a Royalist stronghold, and its last siege began in November 1645. Cut off and short of money, the defenders set up their own mint and made coins from donated silver plate. "OBS" is short for the Latin obsidium, meaning siege. The town surrendered in May 1646 on the king's orders.

A small hole near the top of the Fyfield coin suggests someone once wore it, perhaps to show loyalty to the crown, the group believes. Mark Becher, who founded the Metal Detectives Group 16 years ago, said a find like this makes you "the first person to touch it" in centuries.
## What happens next

Under the Treasure Act 1996, a possible treasure find must be reported to the local finds liaison officer within 14 days. The BBC reported that the British Museum is due to examine the coin before it goes to a museum in Essex. Mr Cedzidlo told the BBC he would like to keep it but is not sure he will be allowed to.
points: Found by Lukasz Cedzidlo of the Metal Detectives Group
Newark's Royalist mint cut its coins from silver plate
The British Museum is due to examine the find

stories.headline: Ex-England goalkeeper raises £5,642 for Mersea charity
stories.summary: Peter Shilton has auctioned football keepsakes from his Mersea Island home. The money goes to the gambling charity he runs with his wife.
body: PA reported on Tuesday 24 November that Shilton and his wife Steph let TV auctioneer Angus Ashworth pick items from their Mersea Island bungalow for a filmed sale in North Yorkshire.

A Royal Crown Derby piece marked for his Nottingham Forest days made £3,000. A gold disc for World In Motion fetched £260. Shilton, who beat a 45-year gambling addiction, set up the charity to help people with gambling disorders.
points: Shown on Celebrity Yorkshire Auction House on QUEST
A mixed lot estimated at £80 to £100 sold for £1,500

stories.headline: Army and Navy inquiry opens into £81m Chelmsford junction rebuild
stories.summary: Up to 75,000 vehicles a day use the Chelmsford junction, which has been over capacity at peak times since its flyover came down in 2019.
body: A public inquiry opened at 10am on Tuesday 24 November, giving landowners and objectors their say. It is looking at whether Essex County Council can buy land, by compulsory purchase if it cannot strike deals, to rebuild the Army and Navy. Stephen Normington, the inspector appointed by the government, is hearing the council's case and the objections on the fourth floor of County Hall in Market Road. The inquiry is expected to sit for four days, with Tuesday 1 December and Thursday 3 December set aside as extra days, Essex Highways says.

Until 2019 a tidal flyover carried one-way car traffic over the five-arm roundabout. It also takes 72 buses an hour, and the council says journeys through it can take more than six times longer at peak times.
## What would change

The £81m Army and Navy Sustainable Transport Package would replace it with a "hamburger" roundabout: a two-way dual carriageway runs straight through the middle of the central island. Alongside it would come a segregated left-turn lane from Chelmer Road to Essex Yeomanry Way and a 350-space expansion of Sandon Park and Ride. Buses would get a new northbound lane on Princes Road and better priority both ways on Parkway. There are walking and cycling improvements too, and the existing subway would go.
## The case for it

According to the council's business case modelling, drivers would get through the junction 53% quicker, buses about 40% faster, cyclists 44% quicker and people on foot about 11% quicker. In October 2023 the Department for Transport agreed to put £68.75m from its Major Road Network fund towards the scheme, subject to conditions. The county council and Chelmsford City Council are funding the rest.
## The objections

Published in April 2026, the compulsory purchase order covers 11 plots of land in Chelmsford and Great Baddow. A side roads order covers the changes to the roads around the junction. The council published the orders in case it could not agree terms with landowners. Objections cover land acquisition, environmental mitigation, speed limits, a business car park and land for the bigger Sandon Park and Ride, Chelmsford City Hub reports.
## What happens next

When the hearing ends, the inspector reports to the Transport Secretary, who decides whether to confirm the orders. Building is now expected to start in 2028 and finish in 2031, subject to final funding approval and other agreements, Essex Highways said in March. In 2023 the council expected work to start in spring 2025 and finish in 2028.

The scheme has already been trimmed. Costs rose with construction inflation, and in March the council dropped a planned 500-space expansion of Chelmer Valley Park and Ride, though its land stays safeguarded.

The hamburger was the most popular design: 60% of more than 840 people who answered the council's 2021 consultation chose it. Councillors granted planning permission on 22 November 2024, and the government confirmed the scheme would go ahead in July 2025 after its spending review. The inspector's pre-inquiry note, which sets out how the inquiry will run, and the inquiry documents are on the Essex Highways Army and Navy page. [Earlier: The Seax's first report on the inquiry](/story/chelmsford-army-and-navy-public-inquiry-compulsory-purchase-24-november/).
points: Inspector Stephen Normington chairs the hearing, with extra days on 1 and 3 December
Drivers would get through 53% quicker, the council's modelling says
Building is now due to run from 2028 to 2031
The Transport Secretary makes the final decision

stories.headline: Essex student Moyin Odeniran wins The Great British Bake Off
stories.summary: The 22-year-old beat Tom Whittaker and Mo Mahir in the Channel 4 final on Tuesday 24 November, with friends and family watching at his local church in Loughton.
body: Moyin Odeniran watched himself win The Great British Bake Off at a watch party in his church in Loughton. "I don't know how that happened, I don't know how I got here," he said after the final. He beat Tom Whittaker from West Yorkshire and Birmingham student Mo Mahir. Tom, 25, had been seen as the favourite, according to the Evening Standard.
## The final

His final began with a lemon chiffon cake with raspberry compote and lemon curd for the citrus signature challenge. Judge Paul Hollywood said it was one of the best cakes he had eaten "for a long, long time".

He came third in the technical, a batch of nine crème brûlée doughnuts. For the showstopper, a tribute to a British landmark, he built London's Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park. He admitted it ended up messy because he went too big. Nigella Lawson still called him a worthy winner, and Hollywood said the reaction from his family was pure magic.
## Who he is

Odeniran lives with his mother, sister and grandmother, Channel 4 says. He started baking with his mum when he was five and had mastered macarons by 14. His bakes often use flavours from his Nigerian heritage, such as grains of paradise and groundnuts.

He graduated from King's College London with a first in political economy, with his dissertation due a month after filming ended. He is also a sprinter, and a former county under-20 champion over 100m.
In the tent he was star baker in caramel week. In Audience Choice week he won a Hollywood handshake for a cheesecake he made with his mother, which he called his best moment of the series.
## The church watch party

On the morning of the final he told BBC Essex that more than 100 friends and family had watched the first episode with him at his church. He baked the cake for that night too. For the final, he said, "we did the same thing, but with more cake".
## What next

He plans to keep the trophy in his kitchen for a couple of months, His dream, he says, is to become one of the best bakers in the world. Applications for the next series are open at applyforbakeoff.co.uk.
points: Showstopper was an edible Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park
Third in the crème brûlée doughnut technical
First series with Nigella Lawson judging beside Paul Hollywood
A county under-20 100m champion as well as a baker
stories.researchNote: Built out at the owner's request, 24 Nov 2026 23:25, from Channel 4's series 17 final release, BBC News, the Evening Standard, the Mirror and BBC Essex. Sources differ on the technical (Telegraph: caramel-glazed doughnuts); Channel 4's crème brûlée doughnuts used.

stories.headline: Maldon Local Plan consultation now open: have your say
stories.summary: People across Maldon district can say what its next plan for homes and roads should cover. Views close on 22 December.
body: Maldon District Council's scoping consultation on its new Local Plan opened on Wednesday 25 November. It asks a simple first question: what should the plan contain, and how do people want to be involved in shaping it?

A Local Plan is the council's rulebook for development. It sets out where new homes, jobs and roads can go, and planning applications are judged against it. Once adopted, the new plan will replace the Maldon District Local Development Plan, which covers 2014 to 2029.
## Why now

Councillors agreed the project's framework, timetable and resources at a meeting on 10 September. According to the council, Maldon is the first in Essex to prepare a Local Plan under the government's new 30-month system. That system is designed to get a plan adopted within two and a half years of work formally starting.

Council leader Councillor Simon Morgan said a new plan was "essential to make sure future development is plan-led". The council says the work remains important whatever the outcome of local government reorganisation, and that it must fit the wider Greater Essex spatial development strategy.
## What happens next

This is only the first stage. Further rounds will follow on the plan's vision, strategy, evidence and policies, then independent checks and a public examination before it can be adopted. The council has not yet given dates for those later stages. Details and the timetable are on its new Local Plan page.
points: The scoping stage asks what the plan should cover
First Essex plan under the government's 30-month system
It will replace the 2014 to 2029 Local Development Plan
Later stages and the examination have no dates yet

stories.headline: Billericay chip pan fire leaves resident with burned hands
stories.summary: A Billericay resident was hurt in a kitchen fire. Firefighters say never move a burning pan.
body: Firefighters were called to a kitchen fire in Billericay at 7.01pm on Tuesday 24 November, Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said. Crews arrived to find the kitchen full of smoke and damaged by a chip pan fire.

The household had cooked chips in a saucepan of oil and left the hob switched on afterwards. Their smoke alarm went off when the pan began to smoke. One of them then picked up the pan, put it in the sink and turned on the tap. The burning oil flared up and burned their hands. The fire service has not said whether they needed hospital treatment.

Once the scene and the people inside were safe, crews knocked on neighbouring doors to reassure residents and to check that their smoke alarms worked. The service has logged it as incident 349633 and says the fire is now out.

Its advice is simple. Never leave a pan of cooking oil unattended, and turn off the hob as soon as you finish. If oil does catch fire, never move the pan and never pour water on it. Turn off the heat only if it is safe to do so, then leave the room, close the door and call 999.
points: Called out at 7.01pm
Smoke alarm alerted the household
Crews checked neighbours' alarms
stories.source: Essex County Fire and Rescue Service

stories.headline: Hanningfield Reservoir hits record low of 35% as hosepipe ban goes on
stories.summary: Hanningfield, near Chelmsford, is at its lowest level on record. It would normally be about twice as full at this time of year.
body: Kieran Ingram, a director at Essex & Suffolk Water, told BBC Look East on Tuesday 24 November that Hanningfield Reservoir was at 35% of its capacity. In late November the company would expect it to hold 65 to 70%.
He said customers' supplies were not at risk, but added: "We're not out of the woods yet." The company has once again asked people to limit the water they use.
## Why it is so low

Essex & Suffolk Water brought in its first hosepipe ban since 1997 on 3 August, after an exceptionally dry summer. Autumn rain has disappointed, so the ban is still in place. Rainfall from May to October was 61% of the average for those months, the company says.

Its own figures, published on its water resources page and dated 24 November, put Hanningfield and Abberton together at 38% full, which it describes as below average. BBC News reported that the two reservoirs held 83% in June. The firm has already put more crews on to finding and fixing leaks, [as The Seax reported on 18 November](/story/essex-suffolk-water-reservoirs-critically-low-winter-drought/).

Mr Ingram said leakage was now 12% of the water the company produces, the lowest on record, after more than 8,500 repairs. Household use is down 7% and business use down 6% since before the ban, according to the company, which supplies about 1.8 million people.
## What happens next

To refill the reservoirs, the region needs about 20% more rain than usual over the next six months, Essex & Suffolk Water says. Mr Ingram warned that use can climb in winter, when people wash salt and grit off their cars and take longer showers. The company updates its reservoir figures once a month.
points: Hosepipe ban in force since 3 August, the first since 1997
Rain from May to October: 61% of average
About 20% more rain than usual needed over six months
Leakage at a record low of 12% of water produced
stories.newAngle: Hanningfield Reservoir is now at a record low of 35%, Essex & Suffolk Water told the BBC on 24 November.

stories.headline: Lower Thames Crossing puts world-first electric haulers to work
stories.summary: Battery-powered trucks are now moving earth on the route of the new road tunnel between Essex and Kent.
body: Four battery-powered Volvo haulers, each able to carry up to 39 tonnes, have started work on the £10bn Lower Thames Crossing, the BBC reported on 24 November. National Highways says they are the first machines of their size to work on any site in the world.

National Highways says diesel has not been used on its worksites since 2025, and it wants the crossing to be the UK's first major project built carbon neutral. Andrea Griffiths of CPRE Kent said any new road is still bad for the environment.

stories.headline: Loughton's Roding Valley Recreation Ground to get new paths and meadows
stories.summary: Epping Forest District Council has drawn up a long-term plan to improve Roding Valley Recreation Ground. Developers' money will pay for it.
body: Walkers, dog owners and families who use Roding Valley Recreation Ground could see better paths, new trees and wildflower meadows under a strategy that Epping Forest District Council expects to approve. The council set out the plan on Tuesday 24 November.

Its list of projects includes improved walking routes, tree planting, new meadow and wildlife habitat, upgraded entrances and signs, and information boards. The council says the aim is to make the green space easier to use and more welcoming, so more people get outdoors close to where they live.

The work will be paid for with section 106 money, the contributions developers make towards local services when they build. It will be done in phases as that money comes in, and the council has not given a timetable or a total cost.
There is a legal side too. According to the council, the strategy is part of its Local Plan approach to meeting its duty to protect the nearby Epping Forest Special Area of Conservation.

Councillor Ken Williamson, cabinet member for shaping the district, said the recreation ground became 'a lifeline for many residents' during the Covid pandemic. He called the strategy 'a clear and fundable plan' and welcomed new building paying for it.
Loughton Town Council, Buckhurst Hill Parish Council, Natural England and Essex Wildlife Trust helped shape the plan. A map of the areas marked for improvement is on the council's website.
points: Projects will go ahead in phases as developer money arrives
Covers Loughton, Buckhurst Hill and Theydon Bois users
Natural England and Essex Wildlife Trust helped draw it up

stories.headline: Maldon house prices up 5% in a year as Tendring's fall 2.2%
stories.summary: Official September figures show a county split in two. Prices rose in nine Essex areas and fell in five.
body: The UK House Price Index is the official monthly measure of what homes sell for. It is published by HM Land Registry with the Office for National Statistics, and its figures for September came out in November. The Seax has gone through them for all 14 Essex council areas.
Maldon district came out on top. The average home there cost £406,165, up 5% on a year earlier. That is more than £19,000 extra, and a rise more than six times England's 0.8%.

Tendring went the other way. Prices there fell 2.2% to £258,932, more than £5,500 less than a year before. It is now the only part of Essex where the average home costs less than the England average of £292,998.
## The risers

Harlow had the second biggest rise, at 3.9%, taking its average to £317,113. Epping Forest rose 2.1%, Southend-on-Sea 1.8% and Rochford 1.3%. Colchester, Basildon, Braintree and Brentwood also went up, by between 0.2% and 0.9%. Of those four, only Colchester beat England's rise.
## The fallers

Prices fell in five areas. As well as Tendring, they slipped 0.8% in Chelmsford, 0.7% in Castle Point and Thurrock, and 0.5% in Uttlesford. Chelmsford's average is now £378,412, and Uttlesford's £465,802.
## Where homes cost most
Epping Forest is still the most expensive part of the county, at £536,719, with Brentwood close behind at £520,447. Uttlesford is third. Maldon is now fifth, £2,718 behind Rochford.

The gap between a flat and a detached house is widest in Brentwood and Epping Forest, at more than £700,000. The average detached house in Epping Forest costs £1,022,897, the only Essex area above £1m. Brentwood's is just under, at £996,190. In Tendring the figure is £366,896.
## Flats and first-time buyers

Flats are a different picture. In 12 of the 14 areas, the average flat or maisonette costs less than the England average of £215,760. Only Epping Forest, at £296,026, and Brentwood, at £264,292, are higher. The cheapest are in Tendring, at £130,581.

First-time buyers pay most in Epping Forest, an average of £415,027, and least in Tendring, at £220,732. The England figure for a first-time buyer is £245,052. Colchester, at £249,711, is the only Essex area within £5,000 of it.
## A jumpy month
Single months swing more. Castle Point rose 2.5% between August and September and Epping Forest 2%, while Braintree fell 1.8%. The change over a whole year is the better guide.
## Essex against England

Across the Essex County Council area, which leaves out Southend and Thurrock, the average home cost £360,791 in September. That is up 0.5%, a slower rise than England's, but the average home there still costs £67,793 more than across England.

Earlier this month Basildon Today reported that Basildon's September average of £367,920 was a record for the borough, [as The Seax reported](/story/basildon-house-prices-record-367920-september-2026/). Our figures match that number.
## Check your area
Choose your council area below to see its average price, how it has moved over the year and the month, and what detached homes, flats and first-time buyer homes cost there against England.
## What the figures do not show

These are averages for whole council areas, not for individual towns or streets. The index is also revised for several months as more sales are registered, so September's figures may change. You can check any area on the Land Registry's UK House Price Index website.
points: Epping Forest averages £536,719, the county's highest
Detached homes in Epping Forest average over £1m
Flats cost less than England's average in 12 of 14 areas
Essex County Council area up 0.5%, England 0.8%

stories.headline: Basildon Hospital gas and air halt 'completely unacceptable', says midwife union
stories.summary: The RCM says Basildon Hospital has had years to make gas and air safe for staff. Women in labour are offered alternative pain relief.
body: The Royal College of Midwives (RCM) says Basildon Hospital's managers have had years to make the maternity unit safe, and have not done it. The union says recent tests show nitrous oxide levels on the unit remain unsafe. It comes six weeks after the trust paid out to 121 staff who had been exposed to the gas.

Robbie Turner, the RCM's chief membership officer and deputy general secretary, said the safety problems with Entonox had left staff at risk. Now, he said, they were leaving women without safe and effective pain relief once more. "This is completely unacceptable," he said.

He said the union's health and safety reps at the hospital had been raising staff concerns about poor ventilation and leaking equipment. The RCM says it is disappointed that, rather than investing in better facilities and working with staff, the trust's decision simply reduces choice and the level of service for women.
## What the union wants
The RCM is urging the trust to find a long-term fix and to build it with staff and union reps. It says investment is needed urgently so the gas stays at safe levels across the whole maternity unit.
## What the trust says

In a letter to staff seen by the Daily Gazette, Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust said the unit will stop using gas and air from Thursday 26 November. It called it a "difficult decision". The trust says it has brought in specialist equipment and followed advice, but air-quality tests still sometimes show higher levels than it would like. Gas and air will not come back until there is a permanent solution, and the trust warned that could need a significant programme of building works.
## How we got here

The BBC reported on Monday that the decision came shortly after the trust's own specialist said a permanent fix to the unit's ventilation was a high priority. No date has been given for gas and air to return.

Figures released to the BBC under the Freedom of Information Act show the problem carried on into 2026. The legal workplace exposure limit was broken twice between January and July. Five people had raised readings in October, although the trust said none of those was over the limit. The trust says the unit is safe for families, and that the health risk is to staff who breathe the gas over long periods.

Concerns about gas levels on the unit were first raised in July 2021. An independent review by the Good Governance Institute found the trust should have treated them as a serious health risk from then, but did not do so until October 2022. The trust said in February 2024 that the review blamed weak governance, poor management of medical gases and unstable leadership. Its chief executive, Matthew Hopkins, apologised to staff and said it was "simply not acceptable that we took so long to act".

An internal hospital report found some staff breathed in up to 30 times the legal limit between 2021 and 2023. The BBC found staff were not told about test results showing the breaches for 16 months. In October, the trust settled claims from 121 staff, 85 of them midwives, for a total of £735,000, and apologised. It says some other claims are still outstanding.

The staff reported tiredness, anxiety, headaches and brain fog after long shifts on the unit. The Royal College of Midwives, which had more than 80 members among them, called it the largest group legal action ever brought by midwives in the UK. Daniel Poet of Thompsons Solicitors, who acted for most of the staff, told the BBC the trust knew about the danger in 2021 but did not tell staff for a year.

Entonox is a 50:50 mix of nitrous oxide and oxygen. The Health and Safety Executive sets a workplace limit for nitrous oxide of 100 parts per million, averaged over an eight-hour shift. It says high exposure can cause nerve problems and anaemia. It published new guidance on using the gas safely in maternity units in February 2025.

Basildon's maternity unit has stopped using the gas before. Basildon Nub News reported in December 2022 that Entonox was suspended there after a leak, while a new ventilation system was put in. The Princess Alexandra Hospital in Harlow also suspended gas and air in January 2023 after finding higher levels than usual, The Telegraph reported.
points: RCM says gas levels on the unit are still unsafe
RCM reps raised concerns about ventilation and leaks
121 staff shared a £735,000 payout in October
No date set for gas and air to return
