body: Gareth Stafford Bull, Brentwood School's fencing coach from about 1982 until he was sacked in 1997, probably abused a number of boys at the school, an independent review commissioned by its governors has found. The review also says the school let down former pupils who came forward in the years after his death.

When one of them raised concerns with the school in 2008, the headmaster of the day replied that he had seen no evidence, even though the school's own files recorded that police had found prima facie evidence against Bull in 1997.

Bull was himself a Brentwood pupil before he returned as its fencing instructor. Published results show he fenced for the school as a boy, finishing third in the boys' senior sabre at the 1974 Public Schools' Fencing Championships. The review says he also coached the England under-20 fencing team, and that former pupils told it he abused other boys while he was still a pupil and went on doing so throughout his time as a coach.

He was suspended and then sacked for gross misconduct in April 1997, after police told the school that pupils had raised concerns about him. He died in May 1997 before the police investigation could go further, so he never faced trial. The review's findings about him are made on the balance of probability, the standard used in civil cases, rather than the criminal standard of beyond reasonable doubt.
## Who wrote the review

The findings come from the "Review into the abuse by David Pickthall of pupils and former pupils of Brentwood School", a 59-page report commissioned by the school's governing body and published on the school's website this month. It was led by two independent members. Louisa Spicer, who chaired it, is a former solicitor with more than 20 years' experience in employment law and human resources. Jane Foster (Sarre) is an independent safeguarding adviser, consultant and trainer who has led school safeguarding audits. They were supported by three governors who had no part in managing Pickthall: Bob McLintock, John Griffith-Jones and the Venerable Chris Burke. The Seax has read the full report.

The governors commissioned the review on 23 November 2024, days after Pickthall, the school's former director of music, was jailed. He admitted 29 offences against 19 male victims between 1979 and 2021, most of them his former pupils, and was sentenced to 12 years with a further four on extended licence. He was asked to take part in the review but declined. It began work in March 2025, and as well as Pickthall's abuse, its remit covered other historical allegations about former members of the school community. That is where the findings about the fencing coach appear.
The reviewers say the school kept virtually no records for the 1980s and 1990s, so they relied heavily on court transcripts and on accounts from former pupils and staff.
## What happened in 1997

The details of Bull's appointment are not in his personnel file, which is thin. Its first document is a complaint from the head of Brentwood Prep in May 1989 that he was unreliable and missed lessons. In 1990 the headmaster gave him a first written warning over his absences and an unpaid accommodation bill of £1,000, while praising his "tremendous success" as a coach and telling him the school was in his debt.

In April 1997 the headmaster wrote to the parents of pupils involved in fencing to tell them Bull had been suspended. A note on his file records that a small group of boys had come forward to a member of staff. The concerns included encouraging boys to shower after competitions and joining them. Governing body minutes from 21 April record that police enquiries, prompted by an anonymous call, had found prima facie evidence of indecent behaviour involving members of the school fencing team, particularly on trips away. By then Bull was missing from home, and the headmaster judged the evidence against him to be incontrovertible. He was dismissed the next day.

The headmaster gave police a list of pupils who had been taught by Bull, and officers interviewed them at the school. On 27 April more pupils who had contact with him were seen one by one in the headmaster's office. The brief notes kept from those meetings confirm that a number of pupils said Bull had suggested they shower with him. Bull died on 5 May 1997, and his death and the police investigation were reported in the national press.
## What former pupils told the review

One former pupil told the review that Bull abused boys on what he called "an industrial scale", including intimate massages, coming into boys' rooms on residential trips, sexualised conversation and invasive questions about their sexuality. Bull travelled alone with pupils and sometimes shared rooms with them. They said he also befriended parents, visiting their homes and having dinner with them. One described him as effectively part of the staff although he was not a full-time employee, coming and going as he pleased, and said pupils talked about him only on a surface level. Contributors said staff must have heard rumours. The review says the full extent of his offending is not known and that more victim-survivors may come forward.
## How the school handled later complaints

Former pupils contacted the school about Bull in 2008, 2017 and 2024. In 2008 a former fencer told the headmaster of the time, who had not been at the school while Bull worked there, that many of his contemporaries had been abused and had suffered mental and physical breakdowns, and asked what support the school had offered. The review says the headmaster's reply contradicts the evidence in Bull's own personnel file and in governing body minutes, and it found no sign of any follow-up.

In 2017 another former pupil emailed the chairman of governors to say Bull had abused him when they were both pupils, and was told to go to the police. The review has not seen the reply and does not know who sent it. It found no record that the email was passed to the headmaster, the safeguarding lead or the police, which it says was by then a failure to meet statutory guidance, and it describes the response to him as dismissive. The same man told the review that another former member of staff had set up a situation in which he felt obliged to shower with Bull. In 2024 a third former pupil told the school it had never held itself accountable for the number of pupils Bull abused.

The review concludes that police held prima facie evidence against Bull in 1997 and that, on the balance of probability, a number of pupils were harmed by him both when he was a pupil and while he was a coach at the school. It found no evidence that the school pursued the matter after his death or offered support to anyone affected, and that its later responses to former pupils were inadequate and lacked empathy. It says further investigation now is unlikely to change those findings.
## Pickthall, and the school's culture

The review found no evidence that Pickthall and Bull worked together, but says the prestige both men brought, as a renowned musician and a fencing coach, may have made school leaders reluctant to believe concerns about them. Former pupils described Pickthall as godlike and bigger than the school, and one described the school of the mid-1980s to mid-1990s as having a culture of fear. Pupils told the review they did not report abuse because they feared not being believed or harming their chances in music. On Pickthall, the review found anonymous allegations in 2007, 2009 and 2014 were not properly investigated, and a misplaced personnel file meant earlier warnings were not seen.

The review also heard what it called credible accounts of abuse by other staff in the 1960s and 1970s, including harsh physical punishment, and of abuse by pupils. It says the staff named in those accounts have died or cannot be traced.
## What the school says

In a foreword, the chairman of governors, Lord Black of Brentwood, who was a pupil at the school in the 1970s and early 1980s, offers a "deep, sincere and unreserved apology" to everyone abused in the school's past. He says the governors have accepted the report and all its recommendations, and that the school has learned the lessons. Nobody, he writes, will ever again hide behind the idea that it could not happen there, because it did.

Lord Black says safeguarding is now the first item of business whenever governors meet, and that the school has changed out of all recognition since Pickthall left in 2014. He points to inspections by the Independent Schools Inspectorate in 2019, 2022 and 2025, and to two independent safeguarding reviews the school commissioned in light of Pickthall's crimes, in 2022 and 2025. The review itself agrees that safeguarding at the school today is strong, well resourced and led from the top, and that pupils describe the school as happy and safe.

On its website, the school lists 17 designated safeguarding leads and deputies. It says every senior school pupil carries a card with the names of people they can talk to and the numbers of outside organisations, and that pupils can report a concern through an online platform called The Student Voice.
## What happens next

The review makes recommendations that the school has accepted. They include publicly acknowledging the harm done by Pickthall, Bull, other adults and pupils, and accepting that the school failed to detect abuse during the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s; sharing the report with the Essex Safeguarding Children Board; sharing the findings about Bull with British Fencing and the British Olympic Committee; training staff and governors in how sex offenders groom children; and checking that no other complaints about current or former staff have been misfiled.

British Fencing said on Friday 20 November that it would commission its own independent safeguarding review into the role, if any, of the sport's governing body and its predecessor, the Amateur Fencing Association. The former pupil who wrote to the school in 2017 has asked, in his evidence to the review, whether British Fencing and the British Olympic Committee were told about Bull in 1997.

Outside the school, Bull coached at Wickford Fencing Club from 1979 to 1987, according to the club's history page, which lists him among its previous coaches. The review makes no findings about his time at the Wickford club.
## About Brentwood School

Brentwood School was founded in 1557 by Sir Antony Browne, a lawyer who later became one of England's most senior judges, and received its licence from Queen Mary on 5 July 1558. Its Tudor schoolroom, Old Big School, was built in 1568.

Today it is a private, fee-paying school and a registered charity, with more than 1,800 boys and girls aged 3 to 18 and boarding for older pupils. Boys and girls are taught together in the prep school and sixth form, but in separate classes from 11 to 16, an approach the school calls the Diamond Model.

Fees for 2026/27 are £30,204 a year for day pupils from Year 7 to the sixth form, including VAT, which has been charged on private school fees since January 2025. Full boarding costs £58,464 a year. Fees for younger pupils run from £16,500 a year for three-year-olds to £23,076 in Years 3 to 6. The school's charity had an income of £44.9 million in the year to August 2024, according to the Charity Commission.

Except where stated, everything in this story comes from the review. The 1974 result comes from published championship results, his Wickford coaching from the club's own website, details of the school's safeguarding team from its website, and British Fencing's plans from its statement on Friday. The school's history, fees and size come from its own website, the Independent Schools Council and the Independent Schools Yearbook, and its income from the Charity Commission register.
## Where to get help

Brentwood School says victim-survivors can contact the headmaster or the chairman of governors in confidence. The review lists organisations that support adults abused in childhood: NAPAC on 0808 801 0331, Stop It Now on 0808 1000 900, SERICC on 01375 380609 and CARA Essex on 01206 769795. British Fencing has a form for reporting a safeguarding concern on its website. Samaritans is available any time on 116 123.

body: The council looked at knocking down Leisure World and building a new centre, but judged that the cost and the years it would take ruled that out for now, it said on 16 November. Instead, council leaders want a programme of work on the existing site covering essential building infrastructure, customer facilities and the systems that keep the centre running.

The plans were examined by the council's Scrutiny Committee on 11 November and go to the Cabinet for a final decision on Wednesday 2 December. The council says fuller details and a timetable for the work will follow if they are approved.

Council leader Paul Dundas, Conservative councillor for Tiptree, said that like many ageing public buildings, the site "now requires major investment". A brand-new centre would have been the ideal answer, he said, but it was not viable at this stage. He said it would not be "remotely acceptable" for a city of more than 200,000 people to have no public swimming, and called the plan the biggest investment in Leisure World for a generation.

The council has not yet said what the programme will cost. Its 2026/27 budget, agreed in February, set aside £8 million to be invested in Leisure World. After the scrutiny meeting, Mr Dundas told the Daily Gazette the centre would have faced permanent closure within months without the investment.

The work would follow the £1.4 million refurbishment of the Leisure Pool, which closed at the end of September and is due to reopen in early 2027. That project covers relining the pool, new changing areas, work on the outdoor flumes, better ventilation, a new splash pad and upgraded water features. The rest of Leisure World has stayed open, though its main pool [shut for cleaning after an incident](/story/colchester-leisure-world-swimming-pool-closed-incident/) on Friday 20 November.

The decision falls during the reorganisation of Essex councils. Colchester has said that during 2026/27 it expects to share any substantial financial decisions with the other councils that will form its new unitary authority.

also.name: Brentwood Live: two people taken to hospital after M25 QEII Bridge crash
London Now: M25 closures this weekend as Dartford QEII Bridge shuts
Echo: M25 QEII Bridge update, fire service rescue two casualties

body: A crash on the clockwise A282 in Thurrock shut the QEII Bridge at the Dartford Crossing for around three hours on Friday 20 November, and two people were taken to hospital, Brentwood Live reported.

The East of England Ambulance Service said it was called at 10.30am to a collision on the M25 near junction 31, on the approach to the bridge. It sent two ambulances, an ambulance officer, a rapid response vehicle and Essex & Herts Air Ambulance, and two patients were taken by road to the Royal London Hospital.

Firefighters freed the two people, who were trapped in their vehicles, and handed them to paramedics, the Echo reported. Essex Police said four vehicles were involved; the Echo reported that they included two lorries and a car, and that the air ambulance landed on a grass verge near junction 30.

Queues built up across south Essex. At about 12.15pm, National Highways' overhead signs showed the M25 closed at junction 30 and delays of more than an hour between junctions 29 and 1A. By the afternoon, the AA was reporting delays of about 20 minutes on the bridge and about 29 minutes for traffic heading to junction 30 from junction 27, according to Brentwood Live.

More closures are planned at the crossing. The west tunnel, which carries northbound traffic, is due to close from 9pm tonight until 5.30am on Saturday, according to National Highways' roadworks data. National Highways has also confirmed the QEII Bridge will close from 10.30pm on Saturday until 5.30am on Sunday, London Now reported.
The condition of the two people taken to hospital has not been released. This story will be updated.

body: Essex Police released the little boy's name and his family's tribute on Wednesday 18 November, five weeks after officers were called to an address in Eagle Way, Shoeburyness. Ambulance crews had raised concerns for a child's welfare there just before 8am on Monday 12 October, and detectives opened an investigation after Blake died.

"My precious little boy was loved more than words could ever explain," his family said. They said they longed for one more cuddle with him, and thanked everyone who has shown them kindness and support.

A 24-year-old man from Rayleigh and a 26-year-old woman from Shoeburyness were arrested as part of the investigation into Blake's death. Both are on conditional bail while enquiries continue, Essex Police said, and the family have asked for privacy while the investigation takes its course.

body: Colchester had 588 households in temporary accommodation at the end of September, 98 of them in bed and breakfasts, according to the council's latest quarterly housing report, which goes before councillors shortly. The total was 550 three months earlier and 472 in mid-November last year, a rise of almost a quarter, the Daily Gazette reports. It puts the city at seven households in temporary accommodation for every 1,000, above the council's own target of six.

The council's half-year performance report, discussed by its scrutiny panel on 11 November and due before cabinet on 2 December, says 616 households facing homelessness were being supported by 31 October. Council leader Paul Dundas said demand for housing "remains extremely high". The pressure has built quickly: the council's own figures showed 326 households in temporary accommodation in March 2024 and 449 a year later, while Colchester Borough Homes, which runs the city's homelessness service, assessed 1,563 new homelessness cases in 2024/25.

The council has turned former private student flats into temporary homes, a scheme that won a bronze award at the Local Government Chronicle awards in June, and plans to buy 65 homes during 2026/27 to cut its reliance on costly temporary accommodation. It has previously said it uses B&Bs only when it is urgent and for short periods. Nationally, the government has committed to ending the unlawful use of B&Bs for families, and a new Colchester homelessness and rough sleeping strategy for 2026 to 2031 aims to step in before households reach crisis point.
stories.headline: Nearly 100 Colchester households stuck in B&Bs as housing demand climbs

councilwatch.headline: Braintree plans £7m for leisure centres and £600,000 on homelessness
councilwatch.summary: Braintree's first budget plans for 2027-28 promise no cuts to services. A gap of £542,000 still has to be closed.
body: Braintree District Council published its first budget proposals for 2027-28 on Friday 20 November. They put money into leisure centres, homelessness and council buildings, and the council says they contain no cuts to services. Councillors on the Corporate Scrutiny Committee were due to look at the plans on Wednesday 25 November, before they go to the Cabinet. Full Council will set the final budget, including the council tax rate, in February 2027.

Leisure centres get the biggest sum, more than £7m spread over 2027-28 and 2028-29. It would pay for pool pods to help disabled swimmers, refurbished pools, toilets and showers, solar panels, new lighting and better heating. A further £600,000 a year would go on stopping people losing their homes, including help to keep private tenancies going and to prevent rough sleeping. The council is also drawing up plans to add dedicated social work support to its housing help.

Other plans include £3.5m to repair council-owned buildings such as community centres, along with more work on play areas and open spaces. More than £100,000 would go on the customer service centre, which the council says faces growing demand. Its council tax support scheme continues, with discounts of up to 77% for eligible working-age households. Together with the government scheme for pensioners, almost 8,000 households are expected to benefit.

Money is still tight. The council forecasts a shortfall of £542,000 in 2027-28, rising to £2.6m the year after, and plans to close it through savings, new income and modernised services. Cllr Kevin Bowers, Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Finance, Assets and Performance, said the council remained "in a strong position to manage the shortfall". He warned that difficult choices may lie ahead.
points: Leisure centres: more than £7m over 2027-28 and 2028-29
Homelessness prevention: £600,000 a year
Council buildings, play areas and open spaces: £3.5m
Forecast shortfall: £542,000 in 2027-28, rising to £2.6m the year after

councilwatch.headline: Maldon drafts guide to curb dust and noise from building sites
councilwatch.summary: Councillors want builders to plan better for dust, noise and debris. A new guide goes to a committee on 3 December.
body: Maldon District Council's Overview and Scrutiny Committee will be asked on Thursday 3 December to agree new guidance for developers. It covers construction environmental management plans, which set out how a building site will control dust, noise and other effects on the people around it. If agreed, the advice note would go on the council's planning web pages. Applicants, agents and developers would be told about it so they can check what to include before they submit a plan.

Councillors on a working group asked for the guide. On 12 October they heard concerns about dust, noise and debris from building work, including whether sites have enough water and power to run proper controls in extreme weather. They wanted a short checklist for planning officers that points to industry standards and official guidance. At a second meeting on 3 November, members asked for more on wheel and boot washing, loose materials near roads, construction traffic, road sweeping and parking.

A report to the committee says the guidance should shape planning conditions so they can be enforced. It is not meant to cover supervising work inside a site, or matters for the Health and Safety Executive and other national bodies. Officers have changed the draft to reflect the councillors' comments. According to the report, the note would bring a clearer and more consistent approach, and it lists no extra cost to the council.

Covers dust, noise, debris, wheel washing, construction traffic and road sweeping

councilwatch.headline: NHS agrees to face Maldon councillors over Southminster health hub
councilwatch.summary: Councillors are worried about slow progress on a planned medical centre in Southminster. The local NHS has agreed to answer their questions.
body: NHS Essex Integrated Care Board has agreed to come before councillors in Maldon over a planned medical centre in Southminster. A report to Maldon District Council's Overview and Scrutiny Committee, which meets on Thursday 3 December, says a date is still being worked out. The committee will be asked to agree the further questions and actions the group has identified.

Concern came from the committee's working group, which met on 12 October and 3 November. Members discussed the lack of progress on the proposed Southminster Medical Centre and hub, and the absence of any update from the NHS. They asked for the NHS to be invited to a meeting, and the integrated care board has said yes.

Water is on the list too. Anglian Water has agreed to attend the committee on Thursday 4 February 2027, and the working group wants to invite Essex and Suffolk Water and the Environment Agency too. Councillors plan to settle their questions in advance so that full answers can be given.

Essex County Council's highways team has offered to brief councillors, after members raised concerns about the highway advice they get and how the team sets priorities. Council letters will now be signed by a named person rather than a team, and debt recovery letters are being reviewed. The group has paused its look at the Prentice Hall planning application because of a possible judicial review.

councilwatch.headline: Tendring adopts St Osyth and Manningtree conservation area plans
councilwatch.summary: Tendring District Council's Cabinet has adopted new appraisals and management plans for the St Osyth and Manningtree & Mistley conservation areas, including revised boundaries where applicable. Planning decisions in both areas must now take them into account.
body: Tendring District Council's Cabinet adopted new character appraisals and management plans for the St Osyth and Manningtree & Mistley conservation areas on Friday 13 November 2026. The decision includes revised conservation area boundaries where applicable. Cabinet also noted the results of the public consultations on the two documents.

The appraisals assess what makes each area special and set out ways to protect and improve it, councillors were told. Once adopted, they become material planning considerations, so they will help guide planning decisions in both areas. The documents were shaped by a series of public consultations held between 2022 and 2026, and feedback led to changes to the documents and, where appropriate, to the boundaries.

These are the last two of the district's 20 conservation areas to get updated plans, which the council's Tendring Heritage Strategy (2020) made a key priority. The Portfolio Holder for Housing & Planning, Councillor Baker, said all twenty had been approved and adopted since July 2024. Five of the district's conservation areas are on Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register, the minutes say.

councilwatch.headline: Tendring's first council housing report flags repairs and complaints
councilwatch.summary: Tendring District Council's first annual report on its council housing says tenant engagement has improved, but repairs satisfaction and complaint handling still need work. A public summary for tenants is planned.
body: Tendring District Council's Cabinet noted the council's first Annual Housing Improvement, Performance & Assurance Report 2025/26 on Friday 13 November 2026. The report covers how the council performs as a landlord to its tenants. Cabinet treated it as a draft and backed the improvement priorities it sets for 2026/27.

The report says good progress has been made in tenant engagement, governance, tenancy sustainment, staff development and understanding tenants' diverse needs. It also names areas that still need to improve: repairs satisfaction, complaint handling, data quality, new systems and settling in the revised Housing Service structure. Tenant Satisfaction Measures run through the report, which is meant to give evidence to tenants, Cabinet and the Regulator of Social Housing.

Cabinet gave the Corporate Director (Operations & Delivery) the power to publish the final report, in consultation with the Portfolio Holder for Housing & Planning. A shorter public summary for tenants and the wider public will show both good performance and areas of concern, the report says. It adds that the report has no direct financial cost and that extra capacity from the recently approved Housing Service restructure will support the work.
points: First report of its kind for Tendring District Council, covering 2025/26
Areas to improve include repairs satisfaction, complaint handling and data quality
The final report and a public summary for tenants will be published

councilwatch.headline: Tendring plans to backdate council tax support for working-age claimants
councilwatch.summary: Tendring District Council wants to extend a rule that now helps only pension-age claimants. Other council tax discounts and premiums in the district stay the same in 2027/28.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet agreed on Friday 13 November 2026 to consult on a change to its Local Council Tax Support scheme for 2027/28. The change would let working-age claimants have their claims backdated by up to 3 months. The council must first consult the major preceptors, the other public bodies that set a share of the council tax bill.

The report to the cabinet says the scheme already lets pension-age claimants backdate claims by 3 months. It says a few recent working-age cases would have benefited from the same help where there was good cause, such as clear proof they were eligible before they applied. The rest of the scheme stays as it is, including a maximum discount of 80% for working-age claimants.

A draft scheme goes back to the cabinet on Friday 11 December 2026. The Resources and Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee will look at it before Full Council decides in January 2027. The cabinet also recommended keeping the 100% council tax premium on second homes and the current premiums on long-term empty homes.

body: Tendring District Council's General Fund was £3.918m under its profiled budget at the end of September 2026, a report to the cabinet on Friday 13 November 2026 showed. The cabinet noted the position and approved a small number of budget changes for 2026/27 and 2027/28. Councillors were told no new major issues had emerged in the first six months of the year.

The report warns that other spending or income trends may still emerge later in the year. It found no other major issues in council housing finances, building projects, tax collection or the management of the council's cash. Officers will review any longer-term effect of the budget changes from 2027/28.

The cabinet also noted an updated financial forecast running to 2029/30. The council is planning for four years in case it still exists beyond April 2028. The report says the government expects to give an update on reorganising councils in Greater Essex by early 2027. The cabinet asked the Resources and Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee for its views.

councilwatch.headline: Maldon council to decide on 25-year River Blackwater foreshore leases
councilwatch.summary: A boatyard business near Downs Road in Maldon uses two council-owned stretches of foreshore for access. Officers say it has a legal right to renew.
body: Maldon District Council's Strategy and Resources Committee will consider the leases on Thursday 26 November 2026. The report recommends a new 25-year lease for the foreshore next to Downs Recreation Ground and another for the foreshore next to Downs Road Boatyard. Both leases would then end in 2051.

The tenant has leased the foreshore by Downs Recreation Ground since 1993 and the boatyard foreshore since 2008. The boatyard lease has expired, but the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 lets the tenant stay on the old terms while a new one is agreed. The report says the council must grant a new lease on broadly similar terms unless it has legal grounds to refuse.

The report warns that if councillors say no, the tenant could go to court. A judge would then likely set the rent and terms. The report says the renewals will not affect the council's finances, and council staff will do the legal work.

councilwatch.headline: Basildon Council heads for £3.8m overspend as homelessness costs rise
councilwatch.summary: Repairs and damp and mould work also leave Basildon's council housing account forecast to finish £3.2m over budget in 2026/27, according to a report for the council's Cabinet.
body: Basildon Borough Council's Cabinet will be asked on Thursday 26 November 2026 to note that its General Fund, which pays for most day-to-day services, is forecast to end the year £3.8 million over budget. The forecast, based on spending to the end of September, has grown by £400,000 since the first quarter of the year.

The report blames the cost of the temporary accommodation the council must provide for homeless households, and in particular a shortage of alternatives to expensive nightly paid accommodation. Capital financing, staffing and the risk that planned savings are not delivered add to the pressure, partly offset by extra planning income. On the Housing Revenue Account, which covers council homes, the position has improved by £1.3 million since the first quarter, with the report pointing to rising repair costs, damp and mould cases and the cost of meeting a Regulatory Notice from the Regulator of Social Housing.

The report says any pressures that cannot be managed by the end of the financial year will have to be met from the council's revenue reserves. Services must now set out the actions they are taking each month under a formal recovery plan process, which officers say is showing early signs of working. The revenue figures went to the Finance, Procurement and Efficiency Scrutiny Committee on 16 November 2026 and will feed into setting future budgets.

councilwatch.headline: Maldon council expects 5 planning appeals this year costing about £500,000
councilwatch.summary: Maldon District Council's day-to-day spending is close to budget overall, with a forecast overspend of £126,000, or 0.9%, for 2026/27, its Director of Finance reports.
body: Maldon District Council's Strategy and Resources Committee will be asked on Thursday 26 November 2026 to confirm a change in how the council pays for planning appeals, where applicants challenge decisions made by its planning committee. The Director of Finance's report for the six months to 30 September says most appeals cost around £100,000 each and five are expected to be heard in 2026/27.

The existing provision of £184,000 is described in the report as clearly insufficient, and because it sits in the base budget repeated every year it does not reflect how much the number of appeals varies. The council's section 151 officer, in consultation with the committee chair and chief officers, has decided to remove that provision and pay for appeals from a new earmarked reserve instead.

The report calls the overall picture positive, saying capital spending is close to budget, debt is being reduced and reserves remain at a good level. Councillors are also asked to agree adjustments for one-off spending already approved in principle, now that the actual costs are known, and a further update is promised in the next monitoring report.

councilwatch.headline: Maldon council proposes new rules for selling its land and buildings
councilwatch.summary: Community groups wanting to take over a Maldon District Council building or plot would have to show public benefit, local support and sound finances under the draft policy.
body: Maldon District Council's Strategy and Resources Committee will consider an Asset Disposal Policy on Thursday 26 November 2026, setting out how requests to buy or take over council-owned land and property across the district will be judged. The report from the Director of Neighbourhood Services and Communities recommends that councillors approve it.

The policy sets out three routes: sale on the open market, sale to a special purchaser and Community Asset Transfer. Each request would go through stages including initial assessment, due diligence, an options appraisal, independent valuation and engagement before approval and legal completion, and the council could use restrictive covenants, overage and clawback clauses to protect its interests. Applicants or buyers would normally pay the council's legal and professional costs.

Requests would not normally go ahead if the council still needs the asset, if a substantially similar request was decided in the previous six months, or if the application fails the criteria. Any sale or lease of a large site would still need approval from Full Council, and the report says the financial effect of individual disposals would be set out in future reports.
points: Three routes: open market sale, special purchaser, Community Asset Transfer
Community groups must show public benefit, support, financial sustainability and governance
Repeat requests within six months not normally considered

body: Maldon District Council's Planning Committee will consider an outline application for up to 159 homes on land north of West Street, Tollesbury, at its meeting on Wednesday 25 November 2026. The application was first heard on 5 August 2026, when a motion to refuse it was not seconded and councillors instead deferred it so officers could test possible reasons for refusal and the applicant could answer their concerns. The latest report by the Director of Place, Planning and Growth says Anglian Water advised that the Tollesbury Water Recycling Centre has room for about 639 more homes, against 558 homes across the five Tollesbury applications assessed together.

councilwatch.headline: Complaints from Basildon council tenants fell by nearly a fifth last year, but most are still about repairs
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Council's Housing Services received 759 first-stage complaints in 2025/26, 19.5% fewer than the year before, according to a report for the Housing Scrutiny Committee on Wednesday 25 November 2026.
body: Basildon Council's Housing Scrutiny Committee will review the council's annual housing complaints report for 2025/26 at its meeting on Wednesday 25 November 2026. The report, from the Portfolio Holder for Housing, says Housing Services received 759 Stage 1 complaints during the year, a fall of 19.5% on the previous year.

The report says 95.7% of Stage 1 complaints and 94.0% of Stage 2 complaints were answered within the Housing Ombudsman's published timescales. Most complaints still relate to housing repairs and property services, and the council lists repairs and maintenance, complaint handling quality, tenant engagement, staff training and new systems among its areas of focus. Social landlords must report annually against the Housing Ombudsman's Complaint Handling Code, and the report notes that failing to comply can lead to a Complaint Handling Failure Order.

The council submitted its annual return to the Housing Ombudsman Service on 29 September 2026, and the report says the ombudsman confirmed the documents had been received and published. Councillors will also see the council's self-assessment against the code and the governing body's response. The same meeting is due to consider a stock condition report and the housing performance report for July to September 2026.

councilwatch.headline: Auditors expect to give no opinion on three years of Basildon Council's accounts
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Borough Council's external auditors, EY, told councillors that the 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26 accounts are all expected to receive disclaimed opinions, and listed borrowing, Sempra Homes and housing among areas of significant risk.
body: Basildon Borough Council's Audit and Risk Committee was told on Wednesday 4 November 2026 that all three sets of outstanding accounts, for 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26, are expected to receive disclaimed audit opinions. The update came from the council's external auditors, EY, according to the published minutes of the meeting. A disclaimed opinion means the auditor is unable to say whether the accounts give a true and fair view.

The minutes say the 2023/24 disclaimer follows statutory backstop arrangements that prevented audit work being completed. For 2024/25, councillors were told that despite substantial work by officers, not enough assurance had been obtained, and a partial audit report would be issued. For 2025/26, the minutes record that the council had been unable to adequately support the audit, with delays in providing evidence and problems with the quality of supporting documents, so only limited work will be done on areas including property valuations, loans and investments relating to the council's housing company Sempra Homes, and the Minimum Revenue Provision.

EY also set out significant risks for its value for money assessment, including the council's borrowing and financing costs, procurement and capital programme governance, Sempra Homes, internal control weaknesses, councillor conduct, and housing performance, including the council's C4 grading from the Regulator of Social Housing. Councillors were told several independent investigations commissioned by the council are still under way and will inform that assessment. The minutes say EY will consider whether to use formal statutory recommendations or other reporting powers once its work is complete.
points: 2023/24, 2024/25 and 2025/26 accounts all expected to get disclaimed opinions
Auditors cite delays and poor-quality evidence for the 2025/26 audit
Value for money risks include borrowing, Sempra Homes and housing performance
Formal statutory recommendations to be considered once audit work ends

councilwatch.headline: Basildon Council borrowing stands at £727m as sale of its Dartford investment property is delayed
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Borough Council's leader told the Audit and Risk Committee he does not support adding to the council's long-term debt until the Dartford property is sold.
body: Basildon Borough Council's total borrowing stood at £727 million, including finance leases, at the end of September 2026, the council's Audit and Risk Committee heard on Wednesday 4 November 2026. The committee noted the quarter two treasury management update, which covers 1 April to 30 September 2026. The minutes say borrowing stayed within the council's approved limits throughout the period.

Councillors discussed the council's investment property in Dartford and its effect on borrowing, and were told negotiations over its sale had been delayed, although a number of interested parties remained engaged. The minutes record that the Leader of the Council said that, given current borrowing levels, he did not support any increase in the council's long-term debt and that the Dartford sale should go ahead before any further investment funded by borrowing is considered. Officers said short-term borrowing might still be needed to manage cash flow, but there was no intention to raise the council's borrowing limits.

Councillors also asked about a forecast underspend of £180,000 from ending the council's area committees, and were told no alternative scheme had been identified, though money could be found from the existing budget if area committees were brought back this financial year. The report says comments from the committee will be passed to Cabinet. The quarter two finance update is due to go to Cabinet on 26 November 2026.

Sale of Dartford investment property delayed by negotiations

councilwatch.headline: Maldon council agrees to buy two plots at Langford to protect wildlife habitat from inappropriate use
councilwatch.summary: Maldon District Council will try to buy two parcels of land at Langford, near Maldon, sold at auction in 2025, and can pay up to 10% above an independent valuation to secure the deal.
body: Maldon District Council agreed on Thursday 22 October 2026 to purchase two parcels of land at Langford, near Maldon, in order to protect the existing natural habitat and reduce the risk of inappropriate future use. The decision was taken at a meeting of the full council, which had earlier deferred the matter until an independent valuation was completed.

The minutes say the plots were sold at auction in 2025 and the current owner has indicated a willingness to discuss a sale. Councillors were told the land has no vehicular access and limited potential for other development but is suitable for environmental use, that Essex Wildlife Trust has expressed interest in exploring a lease, and that the housebuilder Vistry has offered to improve the footpath across one of the plots. The report proposed discretion to pay up to 5% above the valuation, but the Leader of the Council moved an amendment raising this to 10%, which was agreed after an alternative proposal not to buy either plot was put forward.

Each purchase is subject to legal due diligence and checks on title, confirmation of the land's planning status and any covenants or easements, a valuation showing value for money, and agreement of final terms including price and timescales. The Director of Neighbourhood Services and Communities, in consultation with the chair of the Strategy and Resources Committee, can agree the final price. The valuation and negotiation details were considered in private and have not been published.

Two plots at Langford, sold at auction in 2025

councilwatch.headline: New rules for licensed pet and animal businesses across Basildon borough adopted until 2031
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Council has formally adopted an Animal Activity Licensing Policy and Animal Charter for 2026 to 2031, replacing its old Animal Welfare Charter after a public consultation.
body: Basildon Council's Licensing Committee formally adopted a new Animal Activity Licensing Policy and Animal Charter for 2026 to 2031 on Monday 2 November 2026. The policy covers how the council licenses, inspects and takes enforcement action against licensed animal activities across all wards of the borough, which includes Basildon, Billericay and Wickford.

The report says the new policy replaces the council's previous Animal Welfare Charter and is intended to promote high standards of animal welfare and a consistent, transparent and proportionate approach to licensing. After a public consultation, the Licensing Committee backed amendments on 17 September 2026, including stronger provisions on intelligence sharing and recognition of the role played by reputable animal rescue and rehoming centres. The council's Cabinet endorsed the policy on 15 October 2026 and referred it back for final adoption.

The report says licence fees depend on the length of licence granted, which in turn depends on the risk rating of the premises, with lower risk premises generally granted longer licences. The adopted policy and charter are published with the committee papers, with the consultation amendments highlighted.

councilwatch.headline: Developer appeals over lack of decision on 910 green belt homes at Billericay's Foots Farm
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee was asked to say how it would have decided the Great Burstead scheme, after an appeal was lodged because no decision had been made. Officers backed the plan, which offers more than £20 million in contributions.
body: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee considered an outline application for up to 910 homes on land at Foots Farm, Southend Road, Great Burstead, near Billericay, on Tuesday 3 November 2026. Because the applicant had already lodged an appeal on the grounds of non-determination, councillors were asked to indicate the decision they would have made had the application stayed with the council. Officers recommended that outline planning permission would have been granted.

The report says the 56.89 hectare site is farmland in the Metropolitan Green Belt and that the scheme counts as inappropriate development, but officers concluded its benefits significantly outweigh the harm. Half the homes would be affordable, with eight Gypsy and Traveller pitches, a community hub and 3.44 hectares safeguarded for a nursery and three-form entry primary school. The Section 106 package of more than £20 million covers education, healthcare, bus services, play and sports, and employment and skills, and the site forms part of the South East Billericay allocation in the emerging Basildon Local Plan.

Three residents and the chair of the parish council spoke against the plan, citing the loss of Green Belt and farmland, traffic on Coxes Farm Road and Bell Hill, and pressure on schools, GP services, water supply and drainage. Councillors also complained that a technical briefing had been arranged without consulting the committee's chair and vice-chair and without Essex County Council Highways, and it was agreed to seek Highways representation at future meetings. The application will now be settled through the appeal.
points: Up to 910 homes, 50% affordable, on 56.89 hectares of Green Belt
Section 106 contributions in excess of £20 million
3.44 hectares safeguarded for a nursery and primary school
Appeal lodged on the grounds of non-determination

councilwatch.headline: Basildon councillors confirm refusal of 175 green belt homes at Little Burstead
councilwatch.summary: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee agreed the formal grounds for turning down homes west of Tye Common Road, near Billericay, going against officers' advice to approve.
body: Basildon Borough Council's Planning Committee agreed on Tuesday 3 November 2026 the formal reason for refusing outline permission for up to 175 homes on land west of Tye Common Road, Little Burstead, near Billericay. Councillors had resolved to refuse the scheme at their meeting on Wednesday 7 October 2026, and the wording was brought back for agreement. The vote was 5 in favour, none against and 2 abstentions, with two councillors who missed the earlier meeting taking no part.

The agreed reason says the site makes a strong contribution to the Green Belt's purpose of checking urban sprawl, so it does not count as grey belt, and the homes would cause substantial harm to the openness of the Green Belt. The committee was not satisfied that the benefits clearly outweighed that harm. Officers had recommended approval, pointing to 50% affordable housing, public open space, biodiversity gains and financial contributions.
The report notes that the risks of planning decisions relate to appeals, cost awards and judicial review. The applicant can appeal against the refusal to the Planning Inspectorate.

councilwatch.headline: Tendring councillors to vote on sending Local Plan for 1,069 homes a year to a government inspector
councilwatch.summary: Tendring District Council's local plan committee meets on 17 November to decide whether to recommend submitting the plan, with Kirby Cross, Brightlingsea, Bradfield and Frinton sites drawing most objections.
body: Tendring District Council's Planning Policy and Local Plan Committee will meet on Tuesday 17 November 2026 to hear the results of the final public consultation on the district's new Local Plan, held in September and October 2026. Councillors are asked to recommend to Full Council that the plan be submitted to the Secretary of State for independent examination by a planning inspector. Officers say they remain of the view that the plan is legally compliant and sound.

The report says government targets require Tendring to plan for 1,069 homes a year, nearly double the figure in its previous plan. The council aims to submit before the end of 2026, even though the government has extended the cut-off to the end of March 2027, to avoid restarting under a new system. Fewer people responded than at the previous stage, when 628 respondents made about 2,200 comments, mainly because the council dropped two of the most opposed sites, at Brightlingsea and Walton.

The most opposed remaining site is the planned 450 homes north of Thorpe Road, Kirby Cross, with about 45 objections, and the report notes Taylor Wimpey has been consulting on up to 500 homes there, with an application possible in December. A 2,600-name petition, around 500 of them from the Manningtree, Lawford and Mistley area, backed keeping Lawford Tye as protected open space, and 12 of Tendring's 27 town and parish councils responded. The final decision to submit rests with Full Council, and the inspector may require changes before the plan can be adopted.

councilwatch.headline: Maldon scraps area planning committees and councillor call-in as new national rules take effect
councilwatch.summary: Maldon District Council now has one 13-member Planning Committee, with most applications decided by officers under a new national scheme of delegation.
body: Maldon District Council agreed on Thursday 22 October 2026 to set up a single Planning Committee of 13 members from Saturday 31 October 2026. It abolished the North Western, Central and South Eastern Area Planning Committees and the District Planning Committee on the same date. Councillors were told the change was required by the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026, which came into force on 31 October.

Under the new National Scheme of Delegation, routine and minor applications go to officers, and larger or more sensitive ones are also delegated unless they pass a threshold known as the Gateway Test. There is no longer a process for councillors to call in applications. Councillor W Stamp said she did not consider the changes democratic and asked for her vote against to be recorded.

The new committee is due to meet every three weeks at 7pm, mostly on Wednesdays, with meetings cancelled when there is no business. A separate report to the same meeting proposed a revised public speaking protocol that would let ward councillors who do not sit on the committee speak on applications in their wards, raise speaking time from two to three minutes, and allow electronic voting.
points: One 13-member Planning Committee from 31 October 2026
Four previous planning committees abolished
No councillor call-in under the national scheme
Meetings every three weeks at 7pm when there is business

councilwatch.headline: Maldon's share of the halted Mid Essex unitary council set-up costs put at about £26,000
councilwatch.summary: Maldon District Council councillors have asked for a full breakdown, including officer time, of spending on the Mid Essex council plan before the government paused the Essex shake-up.
body: Maldon District Council received a report from its Chief Executive on Thursday 22 October 2026 setting out what it spent preparing for a Mid Essex unitary council before the government paused local government reorganisation. Councillors agreed to ask for a full breakdown of the costs, including officer time, and details of how the Mid Essex Director was appointed.

The report says the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government withdrew the five-unitary model for Essex on 7 September 2026 and paused reorganisation for review. Costs between the choice of that model and the pause are estimated at £78,000, with Maldon expected to pay a third, about £26,000, for IT, a councillor engagement event, staff support and specialist project management. No posts were recruited specifically for the work, and earlier Freedom of Information requests about the costs were refused because the figures were due to be published.

The final figure is due to be confirmed by the Mid Essex Programme Board in November, and the council is still waiting to hear whether there are Essex-wide costs to share. Councillors were also told that Essex County Council has consented to a Greater Essex mayoral strategic authority with Southend-on-Sea City Council and Thurrock Council, though all three must agree, and that the first mayoral election is now planned for May 2028.
points: Mid Essex set-up costs estimated at £78,000

councilwatch.headline: Government direction pushes Southend's draft local plan towards a six-week public consultation
councilwatch.summary: The new plan would set the rules for where homes go and how the council handles applications for shared houses, affordable housing and hot food takeaways.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's cabinet held an extraordinary meeting on 5 November 2026 to consider the final draft of the city's new Local Plan. A report from the Executive Director (Environment and Place) sought agreement to comply with a government direction by publishing the Regulation 19 Proposed Submission version of the plan for a consultation lasting at least six weeks. At this stage residents and others can comment on whether the plan is sound and legally compliant.

The minutes say national policy requires every council to keep an up-to-date local plan, which allocates sites for development and sets the policies used to decide planning applications. Councillors were told the existing Development Plan is out of date and no longer reflects major social, environmental and economic changes. The reasons recorded for the decision warn that without a plan development would not stop, but would be more likely to come forward in an uncoordinated and speculative way, with less supporting infrastructure and fewer protections for existing residents.

The papers say new criteria-based policies would give the council a more robust, evidenced approach to applications including Houses in Multiple Occupation, affordable housing and hot food takeaways. The meeting papers include the draft plan, a policies map, a report on the earlier Regulation 18 consultation, a sustainability appraisal and an updated Local Development Scheme setting out the timetable. Three questions from councillors were answered at the meeting and published with the minutes.

body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's external auditor, KPMG, reported on its audit of the council's accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026 at the Audit and Governance Committee on 19 October 2026. KPMG said the work was progressing well and remained on track to be completed ahead of the statutory deadline. The committee noted the report.

Councillors were told of a £1.7 million unadjusted audit difference relating to pension liabilities, along with several control findings on property valuations and declarations of related party interests. Some risks identified at the planning stage had been removed after testing, but work was continuing on the valuation of council dwellings and on journal testing. Members asked about a fall in the value of council homes, proposed changes to the audit fee and how related party declarations are handled.

KPMG confirmed that officers had continued to support the audit and said there were no concerns about meeting the January 2027 deadline. At the same meeting the committee heard that a national financial resilience index placed Southend 30th of 62 comparable unitary councils, which officers described as a broadly average position.

councilwatch.summary: Electrical safety checks on council homes are now close to complete, but councillors heard that repairs remain the weak spot in Southend's response to the social housing regulator.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's Audit and Governance Committee received an update on 19 October 2026 on the council's progress in responding to a judgement by the Regulator of Social Housing. The report, from the Executive Director for Environment and Place, also covered the council's dealings with the Housing Ombudsman and the Building Safety Regulator.

The Head of Housing told the committee that monthly meetings with the regulator were continuing and that significant progress had been made on the council's Provider Improvement Plan. The council has reached 100% coverage of electrical safety checks in communal areas and 99% in homes, and the minutes say the regulator now regards electrical safety as business as usual. Repairs remain an area of focus, and a targeted improvement plan has been agreed with the council's repairs contractor to cut work in progress and bring performance up to industry norms by Christmas 2026.

Councillors were told the Housing Ombudsman's investigation has concluded, with the council due to submit a learning statement as the final stage. Officers said this was the first inspection under the new consumer regulation framework and that the council knew of areas needing improvement before the inspections took place. The committee asked for a further update on repairs performance.

councilwatch.headline: Three in four Thurrock children entering care now get their first health check on time, up from 36%
councilwatch.summary: Councillors scrutinising children's services heard that initial health assessments within the 20-day legal deadline have more than doubled.
body: Thurrock Council's Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee was told on 22 October 2026 that 75% of initial health assessments for children entering care are now completed within the statutory 20-day timescale. The figure compares with 36% previously, according to the minutes of the meeting.

Officers put the improvement down to closer joint working with Children's Services, more paediatric capacity and better oversight. They said late assessments were mainly caused by changes of placement, hospital admissions, missed appointments and occasional staff absence, and that only one delayed assessment in the reporting period was down to a lack of capacity.

The service is moving to a model led by specialist nurses working with paediatricians, and officers said a formal review in December 2026 will look at the views of children and families, the quality of assessments and timeliness. Councillors questioned whether enough paediatric capacity would remain, and officers said the aim was to use existing paediatric resources more effectively. The committee noted the update.

councilwatch.headline: Epping Forest councillors asked to back raising the top fly-tipping fine from £1,000 to £5,000
councilwatch.summary: A motion to full council called for the district's maximum fixed penalty for fly-tipping to rise fivefold now that the law allows it.
body: A motion put to Epping Forest District Council's full council meeting on 22 October 2026 asked councillors to support, in principle, raising the council's maximum fixed penalty notice for fly-tipping from £1,000 to £5,000. It was proposed by Councillor K Rizvi and seconded by Councillor C McCann. The published papers do not yet record the outcome.

The motion says the council can currently issue fines of up to £1,000 for fly-tipping, but recent changes to the law now allow councils to set a maximum of £5,000. It argues that people who deliberately dump waste should face a penalty reflecting the damage to the environment and the costs borne by residents.

If backed, the motion asks the Cabinet Member for Environment and Regulatory Services to work with the council's environmental enforcement team to bring in the higher fine as soon as practicable, subject to legal and constitutional requirements. It also calls for clear public communication and continued enforcement, and encourages residents to keep reporting fly-tipping with photographs, CCTV or dashcam footage where they have it.
points: Current maximum fly-tipping fixed penalty: £1,000
Proposed maximum: £5,000
Motion considered at full council on 22 October 2026; outcome not yet published

councilwatch.headline: Tendring set to adopt new protection plans for St Osyth and Manningtree and Mistley conservation areas
councilwatch.summary: Cabinet will decide on 13 November whether to adopt the final two of 20 conservation area appraisals, including revised boundaries.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet will be asked on 13 November 2026 to adopt updated Conservation Area Character Appraisals and Management Plans for St Osyth and for Manningtree and Mistley. The report from the Portfolio Holder for Housing and Planning recommends adoption, including revised conservation area boundaries where applicable.

The report says both documents were shaped by public consultations held between 2022 and 2026, and that responses led to changes, including to some boundaries. Once adopted, the appraisals would become material planning considerations, meaning they would carry weight when planning applications in those areas are decided. They are the last two in a programme to review all 20 of the district's conservation areas, a priority of the Tendring Heritage Strategy, which includes five areas on Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register.

The report says that without adoption the council could not give weight to the updated appraisals in planning decisions, and its ability to conserve the district's historic environment would be reduced. The documents are also intended to inform the council's emerging Local Plan.
points: Cabinet decision due 13 November 2026
Covers St Osyth and Manningtree and Mistley, with revised boundaries where applicable
Completes the review of all 20 Tendring conservation areas

councilwatch.headline: Tendring adopts new skills and conduct standards for council housing staff after tenant feedback
councilwatch.summary: Cabinet adopted a policy setting out the skills, qualifications and conduct expected of housing staff, to meet a new regulator standard.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet adopted a Housing Competence and Conduct Policy on 23 October 2026. The policy sets out the knowledge, skills, experience and behaviour expected of council housing staff and contractors, and includes a Housing Code of Conduct for staff.

The report says the policy is needed to comply with the Regulator of Social Housing's Competence and Conduct Standard, which requires landlords to have a written policy, and that failing to meet it could expose the council to regulatory scrutiny and enforcement. It covers recruitment, training, professional qualifications, appraisal and performance management. Tenants told the council their priorities were being treated with respect, being listened to, getting an empathetic response and being kept informed.

Tenant consultation on the code of conduct closed on 28 October 2026, and the cabinet authorised the Corporate Director (Operations and Delivery) to make changes in response, in consultation with the housing portfolio holder. The policy will be reviewed annually and no later than October 2027.
points: Adopted by cabinet on 23 October 2026
Meets the Regulator of Social Housing's Competence and Conduct Standard
Review due no later than October 2027

councilwatch.headline: Tendring budgets for life beyond 2028 as the government pauses the council shake-up
councilwatch.summary: With Whitehall reviewing its plan to replace Essex's councils, Tendring's cabinet has agreed to plan four years ahead, and backed money for toilets, playgrounds and housing staff.
body: Tendring District Council's cabinet has agreed to refresh the council's financial forecast over four years, to allow for the possibility that the council still exists after April 2028. That date had been the proposed start for a new unitary council under the government's original timetable for Greater Essex, but on 7 September 2026 the government announced it would pause and review its local government reorganisation programme.

The report to cabinet on 23 October said the pause had brought a significant level of uncertainty for the councils affected, though Tendring's two-year financial plan still left it in a positive position. If reorganisation goes ahead, even later than planned, the forecast can be switched back to the council's earlier approach of preparing for a handover to the new authority.

Cabinet also approved changes to this year's budget, including £540,000 for housing capacity and restructuring, £100,000 to invest in public toilets and £400,000 for project delivery capacity, and accepted £270,000 from the government's Playground Fund. The report said the general fund was £3.669m underspent against its profiled budget at the end of July, largely because of the timing of spending.
points: Forecast to be refreshed over four years in case the council continues beyond April 2028
Government paused its reorganisation programme on 7 September 2026
£270,000 Playground Fund grant accepted and £100,000 set aside for public toilets
General fund £3.669m underspent at the end of July, mostly down to timing

councilwatch.headline: Thurrock's special needs funding gap keeps growing as Treetops School plans 110 more places
councilwatch.summary: Children's services are on course to underspend by about £0.5m, but the grant that pays for special educational needs is heading deeper into deficit, councillors heard.
body: Thurrock Council's children's services are forecast to underspend by about £0.5 million this year, councillors on the Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee heard on 22 October. Officers said the underspend came largely from making the most of grants and from staff vacancies, which offset rising demand, and that all planned savings had been achieved.

The committee was also told about pressure on the high needs block of the Dedicated Schools Grant, which pays for special educational needs provision. Officers said forecasts showed a growing deficit despite investment in local specialist places, and that national funding arrangements and reform proposals would be critical to its long-term sustainability, with government support expected to cover a substantial part of the deficit.

Officers confirmed that 110 additional places were planned at Treetops School through a phased expansion, which would add local specialist capacity and reduce reliance on placements outside the borough. They said feedback from the Department for Education on the council's submission had been positive, focusing on extra detail and measurable outcomes rather than finances. The committee noted the forecast.
points: Children's services forecast to underspend by about £0.5m
High needs deficit growing despite investment in local places
110 more places planned at Treetops School in a phased expansion
Government support expected to cover a substantial part of the deficit

councilwatch.headline: Thurrock picked as one of seven national pilots helping children stay with their wider family
councilwatch.summary: The Kinship Zones pilot will give practical, emotional and financial support to relatives raising children, as Thurrock reshapes its children's social care.
body: Thurrock has been selected as one of seven national Kinship Zones pilot authorities, councillors heard at the Children's Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 22 October. The pilot aims to help children stay safely within their wider family networks, with practical, emotional and financial support for kinship carers and fewer care proceedings.

It is part of the council's Families First Partnership programme, which aims to step in earlier and support whole families. Officers said ten Family Help Teams had been set up and a single assessment and planning framework introduced, and that work was under way on a Multi-Agency Child Protection Team bringing together professionals from partner organisations.

The committee also heard that 75% of initial health assessments for children entering care were now completed within the statutory 20 days, up from 36% previously. Officers credited closer joint working, more paediatric capacity and better oversight, and said a formal review of the new nurse-led and paediatrician model would take place in December 2026.
points: One of seven national Kinship Zones pilot authorities
Ten Family Help Teams now in place
75% of health checks for children entering care now on time, up from 36%
Review of the new health assessment model due in December

councilwatch.headline: Southend's fraud investigators have brought in more than £800,000 for the council this year
councilwatch.summary: School admissions fraud and Blue Badge misuse were among the areas councillors raised as the council's counter fraud team reported on its work.
body: Southend-on-Sea City Council's Counter Fraud and Investigation Team has generated benefits of more than £800,000 for the council so far this financial year, the Audit and Governance Committee heard on 19 October.

Councillors discussed recent work on school admissions fraud. Officers said referrals came from school admissions officers, members of the public and the team's own proactive investigations, and that growing public awareness had led to more referrals. Members also asked about Blue Badge enforcement and future investigation exercises.

The committee heard that a new fraud investigator had been recruited and that a number of investigations involving council employees were continuing. Officers said details could not be disclosed for confidentiality reasons, but that criminal prosecutions continued to be pursued where appropriate. The committee noted the report.
points: Benefits of more than £800,000 so far this financial year
More school admissions fraud referrals as awareness grows
Blue Badge enforcement raised by councillors
New fraud investigator recruited
